Also, the custom has become widespread in the world that we do not recite a blessing after performing this mitzvah. Any custom around which there is uncertainty, one follows the local custom. This is stated in the Jer. Talmud, “Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said: “In any practical question in which there is uncertainty in court, go out and see how the public acts, and act accordingly.”27JT Ma’aser Sheni, 5:2
Therefore, the sages decreed the recitation of a blessing for all mitzvot that involve reading, whether it is a Torah command, such as the Shema, or a rabbinic decree, such as reading the Megillah, Hallel, Haftorah, or Pesukei D’zimra, because they are similar to Torah reading. But for the commandment of Torah study, “You recite it day and night” (Josh. 1:8), which we are obligated to perform all day, one does not recite a blessing afterwards but only before, such as tefillin and tzitzit, which we are commanded to do all day. Similarly, we do not recite a blessing following the reading of the Tamid portion in the morning,28(Numbers 28: 1-8) It is customary to recite the portion of the Torah each day dealing with the daily sacrifices in the Temple. since it is part of this mitzvah, “You shall recite it day and night;” one is obligated to do it all day as explained above. Also, they decreed that anything that a person has a benefit from, one recites a blessing after it, similar to Birkat HaMazon, about which we say, “You shall eat, be satiated and you shall bless…” (Deut. 8:10)

One hears another reciting a blessing, whether it is a blessing for performing a mitzvah29Birkat HaMitzvah is a mitzvah blessing or a blessing recited upon performing a commandment. or a blessing over fruit, should answer amen.30BT Berachot 51b, Maimonides Berachot 1:13 We learn in Berachot, Ch. 7, (Shelosha sh’achlu): “A baraita taught: If one answers amen after his own blessings, it is praiseworthy. Another baraita taught: It is reprehensible. This is not a contradiction. The second baraita that deems it offensive is speaking about most blessings. The first baraita, which says it is praiseworthy, is speaking about blessings such as: “Who builds Jerusalem;”31BT Berachot 45b The Geonim and the commentators explain that it doesn’t refer specifically to “Who builds Jerusalem,” (in the Birkat HaMazon), but any blessing that is the conclusion of a liturgical section. Other examples are Yishtabach, following Pesukei D'zimra,32Pesukei D’Zimra, literally “Verses of Song,” refers to the preliminary service prior the Shema and its blessings in the morning prayers. Yehallelucha, at the end of Hallel, the conclusion of the Amidah prayer, and the Hashkiveinu (in the evening service). In these cases, Amen is not an interruption since it considered part of the blessing just as, "My Master, open my mouth…” (is considered part of the Amidah) (Ps. 51:17).33The opening words of the Amidah. The Talmud only mentions Boneh Yerushalaim (“Builder of Jerusalem”) as a way of being inclusive, Even though it is followed by (another blessing) HaTov ViHameitiv (The One who is good who does good)34Boneh Yerushalaim is the third blessing of the Grace after the meal and HaTov is the fourth blessing. Since HaTov was added later on, following the Bar Kochba revolt, the third paragraph was originally the end of the Grace and it ended with Amen. it is still the custom to say Amen after Boneh.35Since Boneh Yerushalaim was originally the conclusion of the Birkat HaMazon, it was customary to say Amen at its conclusion as part of prayer. The fourth blessing is not germaine to the Birkat HaMazon so it appears after the concluding “Amen.” Also, since the third blessing of the Birkat HaMazon includes matters relating to the Grace after the Meal, it ends with Amen. The author of Halachot Gedolot explains that it is certainly considered uncultivated for a person to respond ‘Amen’ after blessings over fruit or mitzvot. It is the way of the uncultivated to speak after reciting a blessing and then to taste the food. But to do so at the end, when reciting a blessing, is considered praiseworthy. This is implied in the Jer. Talmud in Berachot, Ch. 5 (Ein Omdim): “One who recites the Shema and its blessings, who stands before the ark, who lifts one’s hands (reciting the priestly benediction), who reads Torah, who recites Haftarah, or who recites any blessing for obligations from the Torah, should not recite ‘Amen‘ after the benediction. One who answers, “Amen”, is uncultivated. Some Tannaïm stay: such a person is uncultivated, and some say: they are wise. Rav Ḥisda said: The uncivilized one refers to one who answers every single benediction, and the wise one is the one who recites 'Amen' at the end of a passage.”36JT Berachot 5:4 The version of the text in Abudraham is slightly different. The author of Halachot Gedolot and Rabbeinu Hai Geon say that after eating fruit and similar acts, one responds “Amen” after the final blessing since it is the conclusion of the act. The Rambam OB”D writes that one does not say ‘Amen’ for one’s personal blessings unless there are two or more blessings. If one only recites a single blessing, one does not say ‘Amen’ after it, even at the end. This was the Rosh’s practice.37See Rambam Mishnah Torah, Berachot 1:18. “Why is Amen not recited after the blessing over fruits and the like? Because it is a single blessing, and Amen is recited only after a concluding blessing that follows other blessings … to signify the conclusion of the blessings. Therefore, reciting Amen is appropriate. See Tur Orech Chaim Siman 215:1 - “Rabbi Yehudai and Rab Hai write that after a blessing for eating food and other such cases, a person should recite “Amen” after the final blessing, such it is the conclusion of the matter, as in the case of Boneh Yerushalaim. The Rambam writes that one only says Amen when one has recited two or more blessings one after another. However, if one has only said one blessing, one does not say Amen after it, even at the end. My father, of Blessed memory, practiced like the Rambam.”

We read in the first chapter of Pesachim: “Rav Yehuda said that Shmuel said: Concerning all mitzvot, one recites a blessing over them prior (over) to their performance…. Rav Ḥisda said: Except before immersion…as this person who has not immersed is unfit to recite a blessing while ritually impure …It was also taught: One who immersed for ritual purification and emerges, says: “Blessed…who has made us holy through the mitzvot and commanded us concerning immersion.”38BT Pesachim 7b The Rif writes that the sages explained that this only refers to immersion for a convert.39The convert cannot recite the blessing until after he/she has immersed herself. Others practice immersion, recite the blessing, and then immerse.40See the Rif on Pesachim 4a. For more on the Rif see ALFASI, ISAAC BEN JACOB - JewishEncyclopedia.com For it has been established: “A menstruating woman may separate cḥalla from dough...” and she can recite the blessing “To separate the challah.”41See BT Bechorot 27a And it has been taught in a Mishnah, “A zav42Zav is a halakhic term for a man with a genital discharge. who experienced a seminal emission, a menstruating woman who discharged semen, and a woman who engaged in conjugal relations and later saw menstrual blood, all require immersion.”43Mishnah Berachot 3:6, BT Berachot 26a Therefore, a zav who did not see a discharge, a menstruating woman who did not discharge semen,” may read (Scripture) and recite the Amidah, and do not need to immerse themselves first. So states Rabbeinu Chananel, the Rambam, and the Rosh.44See Rabbeinu Chananel on this Talmud Passage, Maimonides Mishnah Torah Berachot, 11:7 and Pesachim Chapter 1, Siman 10, on Berachot 26a But Rashi explains that since a baal keri45A baal keri is a man who had a seminal emission and has not yet been to the mikvah. Ezra instituted a decree that a baal keri cannot study Torah, though this decree was eventually nullified. Why should a baal keri not study Torah? A certain level of decorum is required for Torah study. is forbidden to recite a blessing before immersing, and since immersion for purposes of a seminal emission was common, the sages instituted that the blessing should be said after immersion. Even though a baal keri is permitted to recite words of Torah, the custom (of reciting a blessing after immersion) has not changed. We read in Sukkot Ch. 3 (Lulav hagazul), Megillah Ch. 3 (Hakorei omed), and Pesachim Ch. 10 (Avrvei Pesachim): “From where may it be inferred that the word over is the language of precedence? Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak said from the verse, “And Ahimaaz ran by the way of the plain, and overran (vaya’avor) the Cushite.” (II Sa. 18:23) Abaye said: It is derived from: “And he passed [avar] before them” (Gen. 33:3). And if you wish, say instead that the proof is from here: “And their king passed (vaya’avor) before them, YHVH46YHVH is commonly used as a reference to the tetragrammaton, the four letter name of God spelled Yud Hay Vav Hay. It is frequently read as Ha-Shem, literally “the name,” or it is translated as “Lord.” at their head” (Mic. 2:13).”47See BT Sukkot 39a, Megillah 21b, Pesachim 119b It is for this reason that it states over and not kodem. Kodem (before) implies that the act can be close at hand or far ahead, while over (prior) implies immediately before without any separation in time. Samuel generalized all mitzvah blessings, but for blessings of enjoyment (birchot hanehenin), one must recite the blessing before partaking of food, since it is forbidden to enjoy the benefits of the world without reciting a blessing. With regard to other blessings of praise, such as seeing the Great Sea,48In the Talmud the Mediterranean Sea is referred to as “The Great Sea” but this applies to all large bodies of water such as oceans. or a rainbow, or the moon, etc., one does not recite the blessing before one sees them, but rather after seeing them. For it is not appropriate to say the blessings when one merely wants to see the Great Sea, a rainbow, or the moon. One would have to close one’s eyes, then say the blessing, and then see it. Rather, one sees it and recites the blessings.
One might question why one recites a blessing after washing one's hands and not before the deed. One can answer that when one exits the privy, one is not able to recite a blessing.49Since one's hands are impure one cannot recite the blessing yet. The custom of reciting the blessing is done after washing one’s hands for all acts of washing, so that one should not recite the blessing when first exiting the privy, which is forbidden. Also one might argue that after washing the hands there is a “over,” (before) - one recites the blessing and then dries one’s hands as explained in Sotah, “Anyone who eats bread without drying his hands, it is as if he ate impure bread, as it is stated: “And YHVH said: “Thus shall the children of Israel eat their bread unclean among the nations to which I banish them.” (Ez. 4:13)50BT Sota 4b This interpretation is connected to the previous verse, “You shall bake it on human excrement before their eyes.” (Ez. 4:12) This is because "a person's hands are constantly busy,"51Tougher writes in his commentary on the Mishneh Torah: “In general, the Sages postulate הידים עסקניות, "a person's hands are constantly busy," means that a person is not necessarily conscious of what he touches. and since one might have touched filth, the Torah requires one to wash. If one doesn’t dry their hands, it is as if one eats bread kneaded with excrement. Further, we learn lach’mam tame (‘Impure bread’) has the same numerical value as b’lo niguv yadayim (‘Without drying hands’) adds up to 168. One might ask: Why is the blessing that a father recites, “To enter into the covenant…” not recited immediately before the act (of circumcision)? One can answer that we are afraid lest the circumcision become impaired and the name of God would be recited in vain.52Since there is fear that the circumcision was not properly performed the blessing would become a berachah levatalah, a blessing in vain. Mentioning God's name (or a blessing containing God’s name) in vain is defined as when it is mentioned within words of nonsense, for no purpose, and not in the form of a blessing. And if one argues that the same principle (fear of an error) applies to ritual slaughter or sounding the shofar, one could argue that ritual slaughter and shofar depend on one's hand, while circumcision depends on another person's actions, and therefore, a person should recite the blessing after the act. This is what Rav Sar Shalom Geon53Sar Shalom bar Boaz‎ also known as Sar Shalom Geon was the Geon of Sura from 838 to 848. Sar Shalom ben Boaz - Wikipedia and Rabbeinu Tam54Jacob ben Meir (1100 – 9 June 1171), best known as Rabbeinu Tam was one of the most renowned Ashkenazi Jewish rabbis and leading French Tosafists, a leading halakhic authority in his generation, and a grandson of Rashi.Rabbeinu Tam - Wikipedia write. The Baal HaIttur also writes that one does not recite a blessing before any mitzvah that is dependent on the hand of another. Others explain that the reason one says the blessing “To enter him into the covenant…” after performing circumcision is that it is not like other blessings, which we recite to perform a commandment. Rather, it is an act of praise and thanksgiving in which the father gives thanks for having been given the merit of bringing one’s son into the covenant. This is correct.

The Baal HaMaor55Zerachiah ben Isaac ha-Levi Gerondi or Baal Ha-Maor (author of Ha-Maor) was born about 1115 in the town of Girona in the Kingdom of Aragon. He died after 1186 in Lunel. Zerachiah ha-Levi of Girona - Wikipedia writes that one does not necessarily recite a blessing before performing all mitzvot. There are mitzvot for which one says a blessing when performing them and not immediately before. For example, we don’t recite a blessing before sitting in the sukkah, but while sitting in the sukkah. Therefore, for some mitzvot, there is time while doing them, so that one can recite the blessing before the mitzvah is completed. For example, since sitting in a sukkah (can be performed) all day, one does not need to recite the blessing beforehand, but (anytime) while performing the mitzvah. Another example is taking hold of lulav and etrog; the entire time one holds it in one’s hand, one is performing the mitzvah. Since one enwraps oneself in fringes the whole day, one is performing the commandment. Similarly, when putting on tefillin, one recites the blessing while performing the mitzvah and not beforehand. And so on with other mitzvot such as these, it is not necessary to recite the blessing beforehand.
But there are some mitzvot if one does not recite the blessing before beginning them, one cannot recite the blessing while observing because their performance is not prolonged, such as, circumcision, ritual slaughter, covering of blood,56Mishnah Hulin 6:4 and sounding of the shofar since one cannot sound the shofar and recite the blessing at the same time, as in the other cases. For mitzvot such as these, one must recite the blessing beforehand. So writes the Rambam OB”M: “When a person performs a mitzvah, but does not recite a blessing: If the fulfillment of the mitzvah continues, he may recite the blessing even though he has already begun performing it. If the mitzvah is a deed that is completed, he should not recite a blessing. How so? When a person wraps himself in tzitzit, dons tefillin, or sits in a sukkah without reciting a blessing at the outset, he should go back and recite the blessing after enwrapping in tzitzit, putting on tefillin, or sitting in the sukkah; and in all similar situations. But if he ritually slaughtered an animal, or covered the blood, or set aside terumah and ma’aser, one cannot go back and recite the blessing afterwards in similar cases.”57Maimonides Mishneh Torah Berachot 11:5-6

Further, Rambam OB”M writes that any mitzvah whose doing marks the completion of the obligation should recite the blessing when performing it, such as ritual slaughter, the covering of blood (during shechita), separating terumah and ma’aser, making a fence around a roof, and similar acts. For any mitzvah for which there is another mitzvah that follows, the blessing should not be said until after the final command. How so? One who builds a sukkah or procures a lulav, shofar, fringes, tefillin, or a mezuzah does not say the blessing while making a sukkah, lulav, shofar, fringes, writing tefillin, or mezuzah because there is another commandment when one performs the mitzvah.58Maimonides, Mishneh Torah Berachot 11:8 Maimonides language, quoted here is a bit confusing. There are two categories of mitzvot. For the first category for example the act of building a fence around the roof is the actual mitzvah so one recites the blessing when making the fence around one's roof, or setting aside terumah, etc. In the second category one prepares the sukkah or writes the mezuzah etc., but the mitzvah is not fulfilled until you sit in the sukkah or place the mezuzah on one’s doorpost - so the blessing is performed after the “final” act. When does one recite the blessing? When sitting in the sukkah, shaking the lulav, sounding the shofar, enwrapping oneself in fringes, wearing tefillin, or affixing a mezuzah to the doorpost.
Any mitzvah that is only performed periodically such as shofar, sukkah, lulav, megillah and the Chanukah lights and also any mitzvah involves acquisitions, such as fringes, tefillin, mezuzah, roof guardrail, or that is performed infrequently and not available at all times is considered like a mitzvah that is performed from time to time, such as milah (circumcision) and pidyon haben (redeeming the firstborn). In such cases, one recites the shehecheyanu blessing when performing it. If one did not recite the shehecheyanu blessing over the sukkah or the lulav, etc. when one made them, one does so when one fulfills the obligation, and in all similar matters.59See Tosefta Berachot 6:15, Maimonides, Mishneh Torah Berachot 11:9 Thus far, Rambam’s words.
It is not the general practice to recite Shehecheyanu when performing circumcision because it is more common than the redemption of the firstborn, and it is not performed at a set time each year. Some say that the reason one doesn’t recite shehecheyanu for biur chametz, the removal of chametz, is because there’s no set time for it. If one left on a caravan 30 days before Passover, intending to return, one is still obligated to remove the chametz. The same is true for the person who makes his house a storehouse.60BT Pesachim 6a “With regard to one who turns his house into a storehouse, if he does so before it was thirty days prior to Passover, he need not remove the leaven. Since the leaven is concealed, it is considered removed after the fact. If it is within thirty days, he must remove the leaven, as it is not considered removed ab initio.” But this does not seem right, since if one wishes to build a sukkah from the beginning of the year for the festival, it is considered kosher. Why should one recite Shehecheyanu when its time is not yet set?61See BT Sukkot 9a Mishnah: “With regard to an old sukkah, Beit Shammai deem it unfit for the mitzvah of sukkah and Beit Hillel deem it fit. And which is considered an old sukkah? It is any booth that was built thirty days or more prior to the Festival…. However, if he established it for the festival of Sukkot, even if he constructed it at the beginning of the previous year, it is fit”.
The reason found in Teshuvot HaGeonim62Teshuvot HaGeonim: Composed: Palestine, c.800 – c.1000 CE. A collection of responsa from the Geonim. seems correct to me: one does not recite shehecheyanu except for things for which there is joy and bodily pleasure. This is what we find in Tosefta Berachot: “A person who separates Terumah (heave-offering) and Ma’asrot (tithes) recites the shehecheyanu.”63See Tosefta Berachot 6:19 It would appear that he recites it because he is joyful in gathering the fruit. The same is true for reading Megillah and the Chanukah lights, since both involve rejoicing because God took pity on us and redeemed us. Similarly, with taking the lulav, there is rejoicing and personal pleasure in smelling the aroma of the etrog, and in the shofar there is joy because when we sound the shofar our memory ascends before God for good. Similarly, in redeeming the firstborn, there is rejoicing that one’s child was born and not miscarried. But in searching for chametz there is no joy or personal pleasure, since one is troubled by burning any chametz that remains. Similarly, in counting the Omer there is also no rejoicing or pleasure for us at this time. It is for this reason that we do not say shehecheyanu at a circumcision because there is suffering for the child.
If one argues there is rejoicing and pleasure in consuming matzah, bitter herbs, and drinking four cups of wine, and yet we do not recite Shehecheyanu over them at the Seder! One could answer that it is enough that we recite a blessing after reciting the Haggadah, “Blessed are You… who brought us (v’higeeeyanu)64This blessing in the Haggadah at the end of the Maggid and before the second cup of wine uses similar language to the Shehechayanu blessing "Who kept us in life, and brought us…” to this night to eat matzah and bitter herbs.” Or (one might say) that it is enough that one says the Shehecheyanu for the festival Kiddush. It is for this reason that we don’t say Shehecheyanu when searching for chametz, since the purpose of the search is to remove the chametz for the purpose of celebrating the festival. It is enough that we do it at the beginning of the festival. Similarly, one doesn’t say Shehecheyanu for counting of the Omer since the purpose of the counting is to bring the first fruit on Shavuot, as is stated, “And you shall count for yourselves from the morrow… seven complete sabbaths shall there be.” (Lev. 23:15) It is enough to recite the Shehecheyanu during the festival.
And if you were to ask, how about Hallel, which is recited on festivals and New Moon, for which there is both joyous celebration, and yet we do not say the Shehecheyanu as we do when reading Megillah? One might say that it is enough that we recite the shehecheyanu when we say the festival (kiddush). It is not necessary to recite Shehecheyanu for Hallel on the New Moon because some of the months are short.65Only 29 days. We do not say shehecheyanu when a month has fewer than thirty days, just as we learn that if one sees one’s fellow in less than thirty days does not say the shehecheyanu. Also, because we don’t say the blessing of time (shehecheyanu) on the Sabbath, it is less than thirty days.66Between one Sabbath and the next. The Ramah67Meir ben Todros HaLevi Abulafia (c. 1170 – 1244), also known as the Ramah , was a major Sephardic Talmudist and Halachic authority in medieval Spain. Meir Abulafia - Wikipedia offers another reason; we only recite the Shehecheyanu for mitzvot that involve the completion of some work. The removal of chametz is performed on the eve of the 14th and is not the completion of this act. Further, the time of the complete removal based on the Torah is not until the end of the sixth hour (of the day).

What is the reason one recites a blessing for some mitzvot and not others? Rabbi Avraham ben Yitzhak Av Beit Din68Abraham ben Isaac of Narbonne 1080-85 – 1158) was a Provençal rabbi, also known as Raavad II, and author of the halachic work Ha-Eshkol. Abraham ben Isaac of Narbonne - Wikipedia asked Rabbi Yosef ben Palat69Joseph ibn Plat was a Rabbinical authority of the twelfth century CE. He is presumed to have been born in southern Spain, whence he went to Provence and settled in Lunel. Joseph ibn Plat - Wikipedia for an understanding of this matter. Here is the question: “I need a key to understanding which mitzvot require a blessing. For example, when standing in the presence of one’s master teacher, it is a positive mitzvah, “You shall rise before the white hair.” (Lev. 19:32) Does one need to recite a blessing or not? (How about) one who gives charity to the needy about which Scripture states, “Open your hands” (Deut. 15:8), Give to him” (Nu. 21:2,) “Lend him sufficiently, (Deut. 15:10), and “You shall return the pledge” (Deut. 24:13)? How about Shiluach HaKen (Sending away a mother bird) (Deut. 22:6-7), Building a guardrail around a roof (Deut. 22:8), visiting the sick, comforting the mourner, accompanying the dead, bringing in the groom and bride the wedding canopy and one who leaves leket (Lev. 19:9) shihicha (Deut 24:19), peah, (Lev. 19:9) peret (Lev. 19:10), and ‘olalot (Deut. 24:21). It makes sense with Terumah and Maaser that one doesn’t need to recite a blessing when giving them since one has exempted oneself by separating them. But shouldn’t one have to recite a blessing for leket, shihicha, peah, peret, and ‘olalot when leaving them behind? One recites a blessing when giving a firstborn donkey or breaking its neck (but not when redeeming it) (Ex. 13:13), for the Mishnah teaches, “The mitzvah of redemption takes priority over the mitzvah of breaking its neck.” (Bech. 1:7) And how about giving first fruits, shearings of the sheep, gifts for the kohanim, giving a half shekel, donation chazeh v’shok (chest and thigh) (Lev. 7:30-33) to the priest, laying on of hands, lending money to the needy, lending money without interest (Ex. 22:24), making peace, showing honor and awe to one’s mother and father, chastising one's fellow, canceling a seventh-year debt, letting slaves go free, setting the months, calculating the season, helping a stranger, orphan, & widow rejoice on festivals and Shabbat, returning lost property, assisting in loading or removing a load from an animal, halitzah, and levirate marriage. I need a guiding principle for all these positive mitzvot, as they are counted by the author of Halachot Gedolot.70Halachoth Gedolot is a work on Jewish law from the Geonic period. It exists in several different recensions, and there are sharply divergent views on its authorship, though the dominant opinion attributes it to Simeon Kayyara. Why do we recite a blessing for some mitzvot, such as sukkah, lulav, shofar, tzitzit, tefillin, mezuzah, counting the omer, chanukah lights, megillah, while we do not recite a blessing for others? I need a key for why we say blessings on these but not others. Even if one says that one doesn't recite a blessing on positive mitzvot which contain a prohibition (azahara)71Since we do not recite a blessing when observing a negative commandment, a positive commandment which is connected to a negative commandment would also preclude a blessing since the positive commandment is simply a reflection of the negative commandment. such as, “do not take the mother with her young…let the mother go” (Deut. 22:6-7), “You shall not reap to the edges of your field…leave them for the poor,” (Lev. 19:9-10) “If you see your fellow’s ox or sheep gone astray…you must take it back to your fellow.” (Deut. 22:1) “When you see the ass of your enemy lying under its burden and would refrain from raising it, you must raise it with him.” (Ex. 23:5) “If you see your fellow’s ox or sheep gone astray, do not ignore it; …take it back to your fellow.” (Deut. 22:1) “If you see your fellow’s ass…do not ignore it …help him raise it.” (Deut. 22:4) “You shall not hate your kinsfolk …reprove your kinsman,” (Lev. 19:17). “Give to him readily and have no regrets when you do so.” (Deut. 15:10), and yibum (levirate marriage) and chalitzah, “the wife of the deceased shall not be married to a stranger…” (Duet. 25:5) and similar cases.
based on this principle,72Based on the premise that if a positive mitzvah has a negative mitzvah connected with it one does not recite a blessing. why does one who circumcises an adult or circumcises himself recite a blessing? If one is not circumcised, one is culpable for karet. Similarly, one who offers a Pesach offering or eats it must recite a blessing. But if one didn’t eat it, one is culpable for karet.73Karet, translated ‘excision,’ is a biblical punishment imposed for a number of offenses, including sexual immorality, eating leavened products, performing work on the Sabbath and failing to circumcise male Karet: A Biblical Punishment | My Jewish Learning In both of these cases, there is only positive commandment one must still recite a blessing. Karet is technically not a negative commandment. Couldn’t one argue that the Pesach offering and circumcision are both positive mitzvot with no associated negative mitzvah, and yet one is required to recite a blessing? And if one argues that Pesach and circumcision are both positive mitzvot without a negative commandment, how about shechitah (ritual slaughter)? One is prohibited from eating a carcass (nevelah),74An animal that died of natural causes. and yet we recite a blessing?75In all of these cases there is a positive commandment with a negative commandment associated with it and yet we recite the blessing. In the cases of the pesach offering and circumcision there is karet and in the case of ritual slaughter there is the prohibition there is the prohibition of nevelah. Yet these cases are different since the “negative” commandments are not directly the same as the positive commandment. How about a case of nechirah, where there is no issue of nevelah, since the animal did not die of natural causes, and shechitah is its own mitzvah at that time when nechirah was permitted,76Nechirah (נְחִירָה) refers to a method of animal slaughter in which the animal is killed by stabbing it in the nape of the neck or another part of the body, rather than using the traditional method of shechita. This was a common form of killing animals in some ancient cultures but it is not permitted under Jewish law for kosher slaughter. (ChatGPT) even though we now say that nechirah is not allowed. Since a blessing was set for one type of slaughter, a blessing was set for all such cases, so we need a key for these matters. I found this in Halachot Pesukot77Halachot Pesukot (lit. 'Legal rulings') is a condensed rabbinic work attributed to Yehudai Gaon in the Geonic Era, containing chapters on common Jewish halachic themes. It was written in about the eighth century CE. Halachot Pesukot - Wikipedia that one who builds a guardrail must recite a blessing even though it states regarding the guardrail, “so that you do not bring bloodguilt on your house...” (Deut. 22:8).

Answer: It seems to us that these positive mitzvot do not have only one reason why we do or do not recite a blessing. Rather, there are a number of different reasons. One has to do with acting justly. Even though this is a positive mitzvah, as is stated, “Decide justly between one party and the other, be it a fellow Israelite or a stranger,” (Deut. 1:16), we do not recite a blessing because the complainants may not agree with the judgment or may forgo the claim and abrogate the need for this commandment. This is also the case78A blessing is not necessary for these mitzvot. for renouncing property,79Renouncing one’s property in favor of the poor. See Leviticus 19:10 loading and unloading (an animal),80BT Mets. 32a פ׳ בחנם for unloading you must ask no remuneration; ib. 31 a. fr. canceling a debt and or not growing on land in the shemitah year, freeing and providing provisions for slaves, rising in the presence of one’s teacher, showing them reverence, honoring parents, returning stolen property, returning interest, leaving behind leket, shihicha, peah, peret and olelot, second tithes, and making the stranger, orphan, and widow rejoice during a festival, visiting the sick, comforting mourners, accompanying the dead, bringing a couple to the bridal canopy, giving away non-kosher meat or selling it to a non-Jew, burning notar (leftover sacrificial meat), freeing a mother bird before taking her eggs.
Several reasons explain why we don’t recite a blessing for these mitzvot. Some (do not require a blessing because there is no act81Since there is no act involved we do not recite a blessing. such as cancelling a debt or removing a property lien. And in some cases, the master cancels the obligation, and it abrogates the need for the mitzvah.

Some mitzvot don’t require a blessing because they are commandments that come about through a transgression, such as returning stolen property and interest, or leaving leket (dropped produce), shihicha (forgotten sheaves), and peah (leaving corners) of the field. How are these mitzvot similar? Regarding “You shall not pick your vineyard bare…” (Lev. 19:10) And if you gather them, “You shall leave them for the poor and the stranger.” (Lev. Ibid) “You shall not reap the edges of your field…” (Lev. 19:9) And if you completed and harvested them, “you shall leave them for the poor and the stranger.” (Lev. 19:10). If one didn’t gather the fallen grain or completely harvested the field, but left some from the beginning, there is no transgression; one does not recite a blessing because there were no actions taken and because the needy can renounce their claim and thereby abrogate the positive commandment.
Another example is returning a pledge. It is stated, “You must not enter his house to seize his pledge.” (Deut. 24:10) If you came to his house and seized his pledge, “you must return the pledge to him at sundown” (ibid.) If the pledge is collected by a court emissary so that there is no transgression, one still does not recite a blessing, because the borrower renounces his property. Therefore, it is not necessary to recite a blessing because one abrogates the positive mitzvah of making the lender return the pledge. Sending away the mother bird is also a mitzvah that comes to be fulfilled through a transgression (Note: Rabbi Abraham said that this is not convincing, for if one took the mother with the intention of sending her away, what transgression is there??)82Note that throughout this section of the chapter, in which Abudraham quotes Rabbi Yosef ben Palat’s responsa - there are added comments by Rabbi Avraham ben Yitzhak Av Beit Din (signified by the preface, “Note:”) as is written, “Do not take the mother together with her young.” (Deut. 22:6-7) and if once he took them, “Let the mother go.” (ibid.) Similarly, the breaking of the neck of the firstling ass, “if you do not redeem it, you must break its neck.” (Ex. 12:13) Also, regarding the mitzvah of notar (burning leftover sacrifice), it is stated, “You shall not leave any of it over until morning; if any of it is left until morning, you shall burn it.” (Ex. 12:10) All of these are similar to one another because they are mitzvot that come about through a transgression, so we do not recite a blessing on them.

There are mitzvot for which we do not recite a blessing because they depend on the opinion of others. The All-Merciful commands us to bring them benefit. Since they can forgo that benefit, the positive mitzvah is abrogated so that one cannot recite a blessing when performing them. For example, giving tzedakah, tithing for the needy, causing the stranger, orphan, or the widow to rejoice on festivals, providing for the liberated slave, giving meat that died of natural causes to a non-jew, and selling it to a non-Jew.83See Deuteronomy 14:21 See Rashi: “You shall not eat any carrion: You shall give it to the stranger that is your gate:” i.e. to a stranger that is a sojourner (גר תושב). One who has undertaken not to worship idols but who eats carrion. Sifrei Devarim 104:2; Rashi on Lev. 25:35. One does not recite a blessing for the 24 gifts given to the priests (kohanim)84See BT Baba Kamma, 110b, Maimonides Mishneh Torah, First Fruits and other Gifts to Priests Outside the Sanctuary 1:1
because an Israelite does not give of his/her own to the kohen, but rather it is God who gives to the kohanim. In several places it is stated, “Gifts to the priesthood are different than other offerings since the priests receive from the table of the Most High,”85BT Baba Kamma 13a as is written, “I hereby give you charge of My gifts, all the sacred donations of the Israelites…” (Num. 18:8) Since they are given by the All-Merciful, one does not recite a blessing. Similarly, one gives the half shekel to the Most High, and in other such cases, one is not giving anything of one’s own, as is stated, “The earth is YHVH’s and all it contains…” (Ps. 24:1) It also states regarding King David, who sanctified silver and gold for the Holy Temple, because, “It is Your gift that we have given to You.” (I Chron 29:14)86Both in this verse and the one above while the Israelite presents the gift it is referred to as My Gift and Your gift, (God’s)
If you ask: why do we recite a blessing pidyon haben (redemption of the firstborn), separation of terumot (priestly offerings), ma'asrot (tithes), and challah (dough offering), even though they are gifts to the priest? The reason we recite a blessing in these cases is because the Torah commands one to redeem one’s son, and to properly prepare one’s produce and dough (before offering it).87The gifts to the priesthood are separate from the act itself. The Merciful One warned us about these obligations. And the act of redemption and separation is different from giving gifts (to the priest), because they depend on the person and are personal obligations, whereas giving depends on the will of others, and the gifts are part of the priestly portions which God granted them. One recites a blessing over the redemption of kerem revai (a fourth-year vineyard produce) and ma’aser sheni (the second tithe),88Maaser Sheni was brought to Jerusalem and spent by the individual in Jerusalem for a meal that the donor made. because they do not depend on the will or the benefit of others. Rather, it is for the rectification (tikun) of his vineyard and produce that one is obligated; this obligation rests solely on the giver. Similarly, we recite a blessing over the separation of ma’aser ani (the tithe for the poor), because it is for rectification that he is obligated. It does not depend on the will of others nor their benefit, and it’s possible that the poor person will forgo it, and thus the positive mitzvah would be nullified.

We do not recite a blessing when performing Halitzah because it is a mitzvah that is fulfilled because of a transgression. The person transgressed the positive mitzvah of yibum. Similarly, the woman cannot recite the blessing on halitzah because she is not obligated to fulfill the mitzvah of procreation. Just as she is not engaged in yibum, she cannot be engaged in halitzah. It is similar to Rabbi Yossi, who said, “One who is eligible for yibum (levirate marriage) is eligible for ḥalitzah, but one who is ineligible for yibum is ineligible for ḥalitzah.”89BT Yevamot 41b Therefore, yibum and halitzah are similar to one another.
Similarly, one does not recite a blessing for a divorce because “one who sends his wife away is hated by God,” and there is a transgression in it.90BT Gittin 90b, Ben Palat offers two reasons why a blessing is not recited upon the delivery of a writ of divorce. First, one who does so is hated by God. And second is that the transgression is divorcing one’s wife. And if you were to say that one should recite a blessing in the case of a woman whom one is obligated to divorce, such as one who is forced to divorce one’s wife,91See Mishnah Ketubot 7:10 These are the ones who are forced to divorce [their wives]: one who is afflicted with boils or one who has a polypus... or one who waited ten years and his wife did not give birth, in these cases, there is no transgression in such a case.92Mishnah Yevamot 6:6 Some say that the sages did not differentiate (these divorces) because the one who decreed these also decreed these, or because there is some doubt in it when one waited ten years and was unable to form a household with her, and so there is no mitzvah in giving her a divorce.

For the recitation of the Priestly Benediction, the sounding of the shofar, and other such acts, one recites a blessing, as we have explained. When making a guardrail (one on one’s roof), one recites a blessing because it depends on the one performing the act, and it is not possible to uproot the mitzvah, as is the case with acts that depend on others.
Regarding announcing the holidays, who says that the court did not recite a blessing in the land of Israel on setting dates of the holidays? But for us, months are no longer set through the secret of the intercalation (sod ha’ibbur)93Sod ha'ibur involved in intercalation of the calendar. This includes declaring leap years, but also kiddush hachodesh based on observing the moon. The overall meaning of the word ibur is arranging the months and the festivals. but through mathematical calculations. If you were to say that we should still recite the blessing because of the mitzvah, “Do not deviate (to the right or left from any of the commandments…)” (Deut. 28:14) or because of “Ask your father, he will inform you.” (Deut. 32:7)94In other words, according to these two verses we should still recite the blessing because we should not depart of age old traditions set by our ancestors… But since there is no act performed here for it is intercalated by mental calculation (no blessing is said.)
(Note: Rabbi Gershon ben Shlomo questions this explanation since we recite a blessing for the counting of the Omer when there is nothing but mental calculation.)

We do not recite a blessing when carrying out the four forms of court-ordained execution95See Mishnah Sanhedrin 7:1 - Four deaths have been entrusted to the court: stoning, burning, slaying [by the sword] and strangulation. Rabbi Simeon says: “burning, stoning, strangulation and slaying.” nor when administering lashes, because the Holy One has compassion on his creatures as we have explained, “For an impaled body is an affront to God,” (Deut. 21:23). “When man suffers, what expression does the Shechinah use? “My head is too light (a euphemism for heavy) for me…”96See BT Sanhedrin 46a And as we have explained regarding the verse, “So that the one could not come near the other,” (Ex. 14:20)97See BT Megillah 10b - The ministering angels wanted to sing their song, but the Holy One, Blessed be He, said: The work of My hands, the Egyptians, are drowning at sea, and you wish to say songs? This indicates that God does not rejoice over the downfall of the wicked. One does not recite Hallel on Rosh Hashanah because it is a time of judgment.98BT BT Rosh Hashanah 32b We also teach that one doesn’t stop when reciting the “Curses (for this reason).”99Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 28 are often referred to as the execration or the curses for disobedience of God’s law. This is also the law (regarding not reciting a blessing) for the Sota ceremony. (Sidenote:100I have translated הגהה as sidenote throughout since these are notes that were added by Rabbi Avraham ben Yitzchak Av Beit Din to the original responsa of Rabbi Yosef ben Palat. This began in Section 11 above. Rabbi Avraham says: I must clarify this reason: One does not say a blessing for any mitzvah that involves the denigration of others because it appears as if one is confirming the denigration. It is from here that they derive at the mitzvot that are mentioned: gifts for the needy, returning collateral, even when it taken by the court or from the hand of the borrower, tearing a garment by a mourner, offering of condolences to mourners, visiting the sick, and possibly leaving leaving gleanings, forgotten sheaves (shihicha), the corners of the field (peah), and similar mitzvot. Likewise, the execution of judgment between litigants involves loss or anguish to one party. Many such mitzvot fall under this reason.)

But for the breaking of the heifer’s neck (עגלה ערופה),101See Deut. Chapter 21 one does recite a blessing; and likewise for the offering of sacrifices, for the laying on of hands, the sprinkling of the blood, the burning of the sacrificial portions, and the rest of their procedures. The same applies to the pouring of oil on the ear of the leper, and on his thumb and big toe, and anything similar to these; and all the rites of the meal- offerings, over which blessings were recited. However, bringing a bride to the wedding canopy is not comparable to the redemption of the firstborn son, over which we do recite a blessing. For in the case of redeeming the firstborn, even if the priest refrains from redeeming him, the obligation of redemption still rests upon the father; he remains obligated to redeem his son, or the son must redeem himself. But bringing a bride into the canopy, since we engage in it as an act of kindness—if they refrain and do not wish us to bring her into the canopy, this mitzvah is entirely removed from us. This is not the case with levirate marriage (yibbum) or marriage generally; for even though it depends on the consent of another, and it is possible that the woman may refuse, the mitzvah is not thereby uprooted from the man. Rather, the obligation of yibbum or marriage still rests upon him when he finds the opportunity, something that cannot be said regarding bringing a bride into the canopy, or giving charity, and the like. For in these, the Merciful One obligated us to bestow kindness for their benefit, and if they do not wish it, the mitzvah is not incumbent upon us. The same applies to visiting the sick, making peace between one person and another, and comforting mourners: one does not recite a blessing over comforting mourners, making peace, or visiting the sick, since it is in their hands to nullify the fulfillment of these mitzvot. And likewise, one does not recite a blessing over rebuking one’s fellow, for we say: “I would be astonished if there is anyone in this generation who knows how to rebuke, or anyone who is capable of accepting rebuke.”

Neither of these reasons applies to reciting a blessing when performing shechita. Shechita does not depend on the consent of others, nor is it a mitzvah connected with a transgression. “You shall not eat anything that has died a natural death (nevelah)” (Deut. 14:21) is not a negative mitzvah connected to a positive mitzvah (of shechita). One does not say “You shall not eat anything that has died of natural causes,” and if you do, it should be slaughtered properly, for a negative commandment cannot correct another negative commandment. Shechita is different from leket, shihicha, peah, returning a pledge, or releasing the mother bird, because these are mitzvot that come to be fulfilled through a transgression and are a single act. They are all mitzvot that come about through a transgression, while nevelah is not connected to shechita. Shechita is a negative commandment that comes to rectify another negative commandment.101There is prohibition against eating nevelah and there is prohibition against eating meat that is not properly slaughtered. They are not directly connected but shechita is connected to the prohibition against eating meat that dies by natural means. Since it is not a positive mitzvah connected to a transgression, we recite a blessing for it.

And the giving of a half-shekel for the Temple, reason dictates that one does not recite a blessing over it. And the same applies to things similar to it, for they are matters that already belong to God, as it says: ‘The earth is the Lord’s and all it contains.’ And the same reasoning applies to payments for damages, whether for injury to the body or for damage to property, even if the one who caused the damage pays willingly. Likewise, the double payment and the four- or five-fold payment: one does not recite a blessing over them, since they are considered mitzvot that come about because of a transgression .102In all of these cases the person is obligated to make a personal payment. From where do we learn that we do not recite a blessing for a mitzvah that is fulfilled through a transgression? It is taught in a baraita, “Rabbi Eliezer ben Ya’akov says: One who robbed another of a se’ah of wheat, ground it, kneaded it, and baked it, and then separated ḥalla, how can (the thief) recite the blessing for the separation of ḥalla? This one does not recite a blessing but blasphemes God! Regarding him, Scripture states: “The robber who recites a blessing, blasphemes YHVH.” (Ps. 10:3) Rava explains that the reason for Rabbi Eliezer ben Yakov’s (statement) is that this is fulfilled through a mitzvah that is fulfilled through a transgression.103BT Baba Kama 94a The Mishnah states in Berachot, “One who ate untithed produce [tevel], and first tithe from which teruma was not separated…. may not recite a zimmun104If three people eat together are obligated to they are obligated to introduce the Birkat HaMazon with a special blessing recited by the leader. This is called a zimmun. over it, and (this applies) even to untithed produce that is forbidden by rabbinic law.”105See BT Berachot 45a and 47b Tevel D'Rabbanan refers to produce that is rabbinically prohibited because terumot and ma’asrot (tithes) have not been properly separated—but where the obligation to tithe is only rabbinic in origin, not biblical. Examples of this would be produce grown in territories near Israel, which the rabbis included in the mitzvah for various reasons, produce grown by a non-Jew, but acquired by a Jew before it was processed, and produce grown in Israel but under conditions that don't meet the Torah’s standards. (Chat GPT)
(Sidenote: Rabbi Avraham has said: This case is of no consequence. The sages did not say that one should be exempted from a blessing, nor that one who ate tevel is exempt from a blessing, but rather that they should not recite a zimmun (before Birkat HaMazon) since it does fall into the category of a regular meal. Similarly, Rabbi Eliezer ben Yakkov did not exempt one from removing a portion nor reciting a blessing over ḥalla; rather, (he states) that there is a transgression with his commandment, and it is not like others who recite a blessing over mitzvot. How could one conclude that one who eats rabbinic tevel should be exempt from reciting a blessing after the meal, which is a Torah commandment? Similarly, the statement, “An am ha’aretz may not be included in a zimmun,”106There are a variety of definitions of Am Ha’aretz in rabbinic literature - literally “People of the land.” Generally it refers to someone who is either lacking in observance specifically in the area of purity laws. See Berachot 47b - “Who is an am ha’aretz? Anyone who does not eat non-sacred food in a state of ritual purity.” does not mean that the ignorant person (am ha’aretz) is exempt from Birkat HaMazon, but that the Torah scholar should not include him in his zimmun. And in that case, in which the Exilarch and the sages were sitting in a sukkah107BT Sukkot 31a that was stolen, they would not have recited a blessing on it since it was fulfilled through a transgression, since the wood was stolen, I was surprised! However, some mitzvot are fulfilled through a transgression in other places where it prevents the actual commandment and, even more so, the blessing.108Apparently the Reish Galuta and the Rabbis were fulfilling the mitzvah in a sukkah made of stolen wood. Rabbi Abraham is surprised that they are allowed to do so (and even recite the blessing) in this case! The reason for this matter is that a mitzvah is fulfilled through a transgression.

“How do we know that a positive commandment which can be abrogated - even if it has not actually been annulled - is regarded as if it were annulled (and therefore no blessing is recited)?” It is taught in Ketubot, Ch. 3, (Ellu Na’arot): “What is meant by 'he must drink out of his pot’? Even if she is lame, even if she is blind, and even if she is afflicted with boils, he may not dismiss her. But if she were found to have committed a licentious act or was unfit to marry an Israelite, he may not continue to live with her, for it is said, “She shall be for him a wife” (Deut. 22:29), meaning, a wife that is fit for him.”109Mishnah Ketubot 3:5 The Gemara comments, “We say that a positive mitzvah overrides a negative mitzvah only in cases like circumcision in [a place of] leprosy,” or a linen garment with woolen tzitzit - where it is impossible to fulfill the positive mitzvah without violating the negative one.110See BT Ketubot 40a - the full quote is: “Rav Kahana said: I stated this halakha before Rav Zevid of Neharde’a, and I asked him: Let the positive mitzvah: “And to him she shall be as a wife” (Deut 22:29), come and override the prohibition of marriage to a woman who is forbidden to him, according to the principle that positive mitzvot override prohibitions.” In this case, since there are times when a marriage is terminated, we do recite a blessing when marrying, treating all case the same way. But here, if she says, "I don't want him," is the positive commandment (of yibbum) still in effect at all? It follows that since it is possible to uproot the positive commandment, even though it has not yet been uprooted, it is considered as if it is not in force. It is not absolute, since the Torah obligated him to marry her for her benefit. And since she says, "I do not want this benefit," the positive mitzvah is nullified.
(Note: Rabbi Avraham states that it is possible the reasoning is valid, but the proof is lacking.) For by a woman who is fit to fulfill the mitzvah of yibbum, is there not still a positive commandment of yibbum? Even so, she can uproot it by refusing, through chalitzah.
We can conclude from the mitzvah of showing reverence to one’s parents or standing in the presence of one's teacher that since a parent may forgo this positive mitzvah and a teacher can forgo his honor, the obligation of honor is abrogated. Since the mitzvah can be nullified, we do not recite a blessing for it. This is the law in similar cases. Also, regarding gifts to the priesthood, we say that kohanim receive from a supernal table (those who give gifts do not recite a blessing). This also applies to gezelat ha’ger111Literally stolen property of a convert/non-Jew Numbers 5:6-8 This refers to a convert who has no Jewish heirs - if someone stole from him or he died without heirs his possessions are given to the priesthood since their property, when given to the priesthood, is considered “gifts to the priesthood.” We say, “God acquired the principal and gave it to the priests,”112BT Baba Kamma 109b as is explained in Baba Kama. One learns from it that one who gives gifts to the priesthood to the kohen does not give from his property; rather, one gives that which belongs to the All-Merciful, as is written, “I hereby give you charge of My gifts….” (Num. 18:8) Therefore, a Jew does not recite a blessing on giving to the kohen.’ This concludes the respona of Yosef ben Palat.

Some mitzvah blessings include the word Al (concerning), while others include with a Lamed (to). Rabbeinu Tam writes that blessings that contain the word al are for acts that are performed immediately, such as, al ha’milah, (concerning circumcision), al biur chametz, (for the removal of chametz), al achilat matzah (for eating of unleavened bread), al achilat maror, (for eating the bitter herbs), al mikra megillah, (for the reading of the Megillah) al ha’tevillah, (for immersion in the Mikvah) al netilat yadaim, (for the washing of hands), al netilat lulav (for taking the lulav and etrog), al sefirat ha’omer (for counting the Omer) al mitzvat eiruv (for the commandment of making an Eruv).
Any mitzvot for which there is a delay (between the blessing and the act) conclude with a lamed. Examples: (one says) li’haneach tefillin (to put on tefillin), one does so for the whole day; li’hitatef tzitzit (to enwrap in a tallit), since one can wear a tallit the entire day; lei’shev ba’sukkah (to dwell in the sukkah), since one should eat and remain in a sukkah all day. In all these cases, one recites the blessing with a lamed since it applies to the coming time; lihadlik ner Chanukah (to kindle the Chanukah lights) because there is a delay in the time of the performance of the mitzvah from sunset until the last person leaves the market and therefore, is recited beginning with a lamed, ‘to kindle.’ Similarly, one says Lishmoa kol shofar (to hear the sound of the shofar) since there is time to stop between the shofar sounds because the essence of the mitzvah of shofar is based on the order of blessings (in the Amidah).
The reason that one recites the blessing lihachniso biverito shl Avraham Aveenu (To enter the covenant of our forefather, Abraham) is that this blessing is not like other blessings. Rather, it is a statement of praise and thanksgiving as we have explained. The reason that we say Lihanee’ach tefillin when putting on the arm tefillin, while one says Al mitzvat tefillen when putting on the head tefillin, is because our sages did not want to decree one blessing after another on the same mitzvah that contained the same form, one was said when beginning to bless tefillin and the second when finishing for the completion of the mitzvah. And the reason that we say Likro et hahallel when reciting Hallel, and we recite Al mikra megillah, is because we read the entire Megillah without interruption, while we interrupt Hallel to allow the community to recite the beginnings of each passage. We find in Pesachim that Hallel was decreed by the early prophets for all the troubles that befell Israel. When they were redeemed, they completed Hallel.113BT Pesachim 117a Therefore, there is a connection to Likro et hahallel because any mitzvah that is not an obligation is never introduced by the word al. There is no reason given for this principle. All the other explanations are forced! Further, I have questions (why we say) lihadlik, to kindle Sabbath lights, and lihafrish, to separate terumah. For if you say that we recite Al - “Concerning the separation of terumah,” it is not so! For we read in the Tosefta regarding the separation of terumah and tithes, “Praised are you…who commanded us to separate terumot and tithes.”114Tosefta Berachot, 6:19 Further, why do we say “To eat matzah” and “To eat bitter herbs” as was explained above?

The Rambam suggests another reason (for the concluding words of a blessing). When performing a mitzvah for oneself, one says la’asot, “to do,” such as circumcising one's son, placing a mezuzah on one’s house, placing a guardrail around one's roof, separating terumah, wearing tefillin, and wearing fringes. But if one performs a mitzvah for others, such as circumcising someone’s son, putting a mezuzah on one’s fellow’s house, placing a guardrail around your neighbor’s roof, or separating terumah for one’s fellow, one says “Concerning the act of…” (al ha’asiyah). For instance, one says, “Concerning the mitzvah of eiruv” ("al mitzvah eiruv”) when setting up an eiruv.115An eiruv is a ritual halakhic enclosure made for the purpose of allowing activities which are normally prohibited on Shabbat such as carrying objects from a private domain to a semi-public domain, and transporting objects four cubits or more within a semi-public domain. But if it was an obligation for oneself and others, then one says la’asot… (to perform the act). Therefore, we say, Lishmoa kol Shofar, “To hear the sound of the Shofar.” When one takes a lulav and etrog, one recites the blessing “concerning the taking of the lulav,” since when one lifts it, one fulfills one’s obligation but one recites a blessing, “To take the lulav,” before shaking the lulav just as one recites the blessing leishev basukkah, “To sit in the sukkah” (when sitting in the sukkah).116Apparently simply handling the Lulav and etrog requires a blessing since the Torah states “One the first day of the festival you shall take…” Simply handling it might be considered fulfilling the mitzvah. A separate blessing is required when you take hold of the lulav and etrog to shake it in the context of prayer.. From this one learns that if one recites the blessing after having performed the mitzvah without a blessing says “ (Al) concerning the doing…” But when washing one’s hands or performing ritual slaughter, since the blessing gives permission, even if one is slaughtering for oneself, one says, “Al regarding the slaughter,” “Al regarding the covering up of blood,” or “Al regarding the washing of hands.” Similarly, one says, “Al regarding the removal of chametz,” whether one does so for oneself or others since the act of nullification is completed in his heart before one searches - this completes the Rambam.
The Ra’avad117Abraham ben David (1125-1198), also known by the abbreviation Ra’avad was an important commentator on the Talmud, Sefer Halachot of Isaac Alfasi, and the Mishneh Torah of Maimonides disagreed; this is his statement: Rabbi Avraham said: it is difficult for me to understand (the Rambam regarding)Al Mikra Megillah, “Concerning the reading of the Megillah.” For if you say Al, “concerning,” for any rabbinic mitzvah, because it is giving permission (to perform the act), then why do we say lihadlik for the lighting of Chanukah candles? It could be that it is because there is no set time, the strict add more time (for the candles to burn), and the extra strict even more. Or maybe the blessing for candle lighting is different because it was based on the kindling of lights in the Temple, which is found in the Torah; as a result, we treat it like a Torah commandment. Whichever explanation one accepts, the question of Al achilat matzah and al achilat maror118The blessings for eating matzah and maror at the Passover Seder. Since these are Torah commandments we should say Le’chol matzah and le’echol maror instead of Al Achilat… remains difficult. One wonders why the one who says liva’er chametz in the Talmud? It makes sense to conclude that we say Le’echol in these cases, since one says borei peri ha’adama, “Who created the fruit of the earth,” for the bitter herbs, one should also say Le’echol maror. The blessings for the hand and head tefillin are also difficult, based on the Rambam's explanation.115They should also be Al, “Concerning,” according to the Ra’avad depending on whether one is doing it for oneself or for others.

Some say that there is another reason (why a mitzvah blessing is prefaced with al or li). One prefaces a blessing with al, “Concerning…” for any mitzvah that can be performed by an agent and refers to a coming future act.120The Hebrew word is להבא - it implies that when one recites the blessing, one immediately performs the act afterwards. And one recites li, “to…” for any mitzvah which cannot be performed by an agent and refers to a future act. There is a partial explanation in Pesachim Ch. 1, regarding the removal of chametz.121BT Pesachim 7a-b “Rav Yehuda said: One who searches for leaven must recite a blessing. What blessing does he recite? Rav Pappi said in the name of Rava that one recites: Who has made us holy ….commanded us to remove leavened bread. Rav Pappa said in the name of Rava: One should recite: Concerning the removal of leavened bread.” I have quoted extensively from Steinsaltz’s translation in Sefaria since Abudraham quotes the Talmud here. No one disagrees that Liva’er, “to remove chametz,” refers to a coming (future) act. Rather, the sages disagree about al biur, “Concerning the removal of chametz.” They ask, “According to those who argue that we say, 'to remove chametz,' then why do we say, 'Blessed are You…Who has made us holy through mitzvot and commanded us (al) concerning circumcision.”122BT Pesachim ibid. Apparently, the blessing for circumcision refers to a future act even though it begins “Concerning the act of circumcision.” However since the father can appoint someone else to circumcise his son, it uses the language al, “concerning…” The blessing states “to circumcise.” Is there no alternative to the boy’s father circumcising his son? The Gemara continues: “In a case where the father circumcises his son, what can be said? Yes, it is indeed so.123BT Pesachim Ibid If the father himself performs the circumcision he in fact recites the blessing with a lamed, Lamul: “And commanded us to circumcise.” But when the circumcision is performed by a mohel then the blessing is al…. The Gemara asks, what does the father of the child say? It answers, when a father performs the circumcision, then he recites the blessing Lamul, ‘to circumcise’ (with a lamed). But according to those who say the formula (for the removal of chametz) is al biur chametz, ‘concerning the removal of chametz,‘ then in this case, even the father of the child says al hamilah, ‘concerning the circumcision,’ as Rashi explains.124Since the father is not the only one who can perform the circumcision, the blessing is Al hamilah for either the father or the mohel. Only when the father is the only one who can perform this act is the blessing changed to lamul.
It is for this reason that one says le’echol… ‘To eat matzah,’ and le’echol… ‘To eat maror.” An agent can't perform these acts for someone else, and also because the blessing refers to a future act. This is what is stated in the final chapter of Pesachim (Arvei Pesachim) in the older and more correct versions (of the text). Also, it is the text Rab Amram brings in his prayer book.125BT Pesachim 114b Our text says עַל אֲכִילַת מָרוֹר however there are other version of the text that state לאכול מרור. In his commentary on the Haggadah this is the version of the text that Abudraham uses. Furthermore, we read at the end of Tosefta Pesachim: What is the blessing on the Pesach sacrifice? “Blessed [...] who has sanctified us with His commandments and has commanded us to eat (le’echol) the Pesach sacrifice. What is the blessing on the [other] offerings? Blessed [...] who has sanctified us with His commandments and has commanded us to eat (le’echol) the offering.”126Tosefta Pesachim 10:8 This also makes sense based on the questions raised for the earlier reasons we gave: why is the blessing for tefillin shel rosh (head tefillin) different from the blessing for tefillin shel yad (arm tefillin)? It makes sense to say להניח תפילין (‘to put on tefillin’) because it is impossible for an agent to put the tefillin on for a person, and also because the blessing is for a future act - therefore, one makes the statement with a lamed (להניח תפילין). And על מצות תפילין (‘concerning the mitzvah of tefillin’) also makes sense since one has already put on the arm tefillin, so that when one puts on the head tefillin, one is not performing a future act but continuing an act one has already performed. Therefore, one says al, ‘concerning…”
How about127Each of the next several passages contain the same structure; they are prefaced with Im tomar, ‘if you were to say,’ and they then answer the question with yesh lomar, ‘one may say.’ This is a common formula used in rabbinic literature for questions and answers. I have taken some liberty in translating it: “How about…One can answer….” Chanukah lights? It can be performed by an agent, and it is recited for a future act, so one prefaces the blessing with a lamed (lihadlik, to kindle the Chanukah lights)? One can answer that the lighting itself is a mitzvah, and since the person uses their own oil and wick, as stated in Shabbat, Ch. 2, (Bameh Madlikin),128BT Shabbat 24a that one must contribute coins (to jointly perform the mitzvah) — we do not consider it as something that can be done by a messenger. Therefore, we recite the blessing with a lamed, 'lehadlik'. Also, it is common that every person lights in their own home, due to the preciousness of the miracle, so the same similar to the Shabbat candle."129And therefore one recites the blessing with a lamed, lihadlik.
How about immersing oneself (in a mikvah) or ritually washing one's hands? An agent cannot perform these acts for another person, and yet the blessing is recited with al, ‘Concerning…’ ?130One says al netilat yadaim, ‘Concerning the washing of hands’ for washing and al hatevilah, ‘Concerning immersion,’ for the mikvah. One can answer that the blessing is not for a coming act but for an act that is already being performed, as explained above.131One recites these blessing after performing the act. Therefore, one prefaces the blessing with al. Or one might say that since immersing utensils can be performed by an agent, the sages did not differentiate between the different occasions one recites the blessings.
How about (the blessing for) the covering of blood?132Following shechita, the ritual slaughter of an animal, one is obligated to perform kisui hadam, ‘covering the blood’ when one who has slaughtered a bird or wild animal to cover the initial blood which pours out at the time of slaughter with dust or earth. See Leviticus 17:13 It is impossible to perform this mitzvah through an agent, and yet one says, “Al…concerning the covering of blood.’ One can answer that the ‘covering of blood’ is the completion of a mitzah, and we do not call this a future act but rather a past act. One can still recite the blessing after the covering of the blood, since one has already recited the blessing for shechita (the ritual slaughter).
How about the mitzvah of the Omer (of grain)? An agent can't perform this act for another, and yet the blessing is “al… concerning the counting of the omer.” One can answer that since one has already offered the Omer, the grain offering, it is not for a future act but for a past act, so one says the blessing with al.
How about the blessing leishev baSukkah, “To dwell in the sukkah?” This blessing is prefaced by a lamed because it is impossible to perform the mitzvah through an agent, and the blessing is for a future act since the essence of the mitzvah is eating, sleeping, and dwelling in a sukkah. Al HaMilah (for circumcision), al mitzvat eiruv (for making a Shabbat boundary), and al hashichitah (for ritual slaughter) are also prefaced with the word al, ‘Concerning’, because an agent can perform these acts for another, and the blessing is for a future act.
How about the blessing recited by the father at a circumcision, who says, lihachniso bivrito shel Avraham Aveenu, ‘To bring this child into the covenant of our father Abraham?” It can be recited by an agent when the father is not in the city, and yet it is prefaced with a lamed! One can answer since the blessing is recited following circumcision and not before, we preface the blessing with a lamed. We have already explained the reason above.
How about holding the lulav & etrog? An agent cannot perform this commandment for another, and yet one prefaces the blessing with al, ‘concerning.’ One can answer the reason we say al is because one can only recite the blessing after the fact, since one takes hold of the lulav first, before the shaking.
How about the sounding of the shofar? It is possible to fulfill this mitzvah through an agent, and yet one prefaces the blessing with a lamed. One can answer, since the hearing of the shofar is the mitzvah, and one can only hear the shofar through an agent, we do not consider ‘agency.’ Hearing cannot be performed through an agent; therefore, we preface the blessing with a lamed.
How about reading of Megillah? One cannot hear the Megillah through another and only with one's own ear, but one still prefaces the blessing with al, ‘concerning.’ One can answer, does not recite a blessing to ‘hear’ of the Megillah, but to read the Megillah, through an agent, an agent, and so, one prefaces the blessing with a lamed.
How about reading Hallel? It is possible to fulfill this mitzvah through an agent, and yet we preface the blessing with a lamed! One can answer that each person must recite the opening of each chapter and also Hodo, Ana Adonai. If one cannot recite Hallel, an agent can do so; therefore, we preface the blessing with a lamed. However, the blessing for Torah study is especially difficult. It is impossible to do so through an agent, and it is for a future act, and yet some say “al… concerning.” Some say La’asok bidivrei Torah, “To busy oneself with words of Torah.”133Apparently there are two traditions for this blessing - one with Al Divrei Torah concerning the words of Torah, and the other with a Lamed, La’asok Bidvrei Torah, to engage in the study of Torah. See Reem edition of Abudraham, Volume One, Note 243. Also see 229-233 in Volume One page 155 We can answer that this mitzvah can also be performed through an agent, since one person can help many people fulfill their obligation.

Blessings begin with Baruch (attah Adonai…) and conclude Baruch (attah Adonai…) except for a few exceptions, which begin with Baruch (attah Adonai…) but don’t conclude with Baruch… such as the blessing for fruits and for mitzvot which have a shortened formula. And there are some blessings which conclude with Baruch (attah Adonai…) but don’t begin with Baruch… such as a blessing that is juxtaposed to another blessing. In such a case, the previous blessing (which began and ended with Baruch) exempts the following blessing from beginning with Baruch. There are many difficulties with this principle. For example, Elohai Neshama, which is not juxtaposed to another blessing, does not begin with Baruch… also, the seven marriage blessings. “Who created humanity in His image, opens with Baruch… even though it is juxtaposed to the blessing before it, and also other blessings (in the sheva berachot). I will explain the order of blessings one by one with God’s help.

We read in Pesachim, Ch. 10 (Arvei Pesachim), Samuel said: One who recites havdala must say an expression that is similar to the conclusion as part of the chatimah of the blessing, to emphasize the connection between the blessing and its conclusion. And the scholars of Pumbedita say that one must say a phrase similar to the beginnings of blessings near their conclusions.” The law is established according to Samuel.134BT Pesachim 104a. However the statement is different in the Talmud. See the Rif, Pesachim 21a
We read in Berachot, Ch. 6 (Keitzad Mevarchim), Rav said: Any blessing that does not contain God’s name is not a blessing. And Rabbi Yoḥanan said: Any blessing that does not mention God’s sovereignty is not a blessing. Abaye said: It makes sense according to Rav, as was taught, “I did not transgress your mitzvot and I did not forget” (Deut. 26:13). “I did not transgress,” means, I did not refrain from blessing You and “I did not forget,” means, I did not forget to mention God’s name in the blessing ….And Rabbi Yoḥanan would say: Emend the baraita: And I did not forget to mention Your name and Your sovereignty; indicating that a blessing must mention both God’s name and sovereignty.135BT Berachot 40b Some rule that the law is according to Rav, since Abaye said: ‘It makes sense according to Rav,’ but Rabbeinu Hai, the Rif, and Rambam ruled that if a blessing does not mention God’s name and sovereignty, it is not a blessing. It must be mentioned specifically at the beginning of the blessing. At the end of the blessing, however, it is not necessary to mention God’s name and sovereignty when it is a juxtaposed blessing. In the Jer. Talmud, Berachot, Ch. 9 (HaRoeh), “Rebbi Zeïra and Rebbi Yehudah said in the name of Rav: Any blessing without mention of the Sovereignty is not a benediction. Rebbi Tanḥuma said, I shall give the reason: 'I shall elevate You, my God, O King!”(Ps. 145:1) Rava said, One has to say, “You,” but Samuel said, One also has to say Elohainu.”136JT Berachot 9:1 Note small but significant variations (in bold type) in the text as it appears in the Talmud: “Rebbi Zeïra and Rebbi Yehudah in the name of Rav: Any benediction without mention of the Sovereignty is no benediction. Rebbi Tanḥuma said, I shall give the reason (Ps. 145:1): “I shall elevate You, my God, o King!” Rav said, one has to say “You,” but Samuel said, one does not have to say “You.” And in the Midrash137There does not appear to be a source for this Midrash. it states, “From where do we know that we must mention God’s name? “Blessed are You, YHVH; teach me in Your laws.” (Ps 119:12) And it is also written, “For the name of YHVH proclaim.” (Deut. 32:3) From where do we learn that one must mention God’s sovereignty? It is stated, “I shall elevate You, my God, O King!” (Ps. 145:1) From where do we learn that one responds, Amen, to the one who recites the blessing? It is stated, “For the name of YHVH I proclaim; Give glory to our God! (Deut. 32:3) Said Moses to Israel, “When I recite a blessing, you must answer Amen.”
How about the first blessing of the Amidah Prayer and the seven-fold blessing recited on Friday night? They do not contain a mention of God’s sovereignty. One can answer that Ha’El HaGadol, the Great God, is considered an expression of sovereignty, as is stated in Rosh Hashanah (Ch. 4): “The verse: “Hear, O Israel” (Deut. 6:4) is considered like a verse of Sovereignty.138BT Rosh Hashanah 32b It is not clear how this answers the question since we do not recite the Shema in the first blessing of the Amidah. Some say that “The God of Abraham” is considered a statement of sovereignty because God still did not rule over the world until Abraham came and made known God’s nature to the world. This is what is written, “YHVH, God of heaven, took me from my father’s house.” (Gen. 24:7)

We learn in Berachot, Ch. 7 (Shelosha Sh’achlu) that one should not conclude a blessing with two themes. For instance, one should not mention both Moshia Yisrael (Redeemer of Israel) and Boneh Yerushalaim139The Talmud is speaking about the third blessing of Birkat HaMazon: However this sounds more like the 14th blessing of the Amidah, “Return in mercy to Jerusalem, Your city, and dwell therein as You have spoken; and rebuild it soon, in our days, as an everlasting structure, and may You speedily establish the throne of David therein. Blessed are You, Adonoy, Builder of Jerusalem.” Since it mentions both the rebuilding of Jerusalem and the establishment of the Davidic house, the rabbis debated whether this blessing should mention both topics in the concluding blessing (‘Builder of Jerusalem’) in one blessing because one does not perform mitzvot in bundles.140See BT Berachot 49a and Pesachim 102b Instead, one acknowledges each separately. The sages asked about Al ha’aretz v’al hamazon (‘On the land and the food’).141The second blessing of the Birkat HaMazon. In all of these following expressions in the concluding blessing has multiple items. In each case the argument is made that they are all connected so that they are really one. It is one blessing because it is the land that produces food. Al ha’aretz v’al hapeirot (‘For the land and the fruits’), one blessing because it is the land that produces fruit.142BT Berachot 49a Mikadesh Yisrael v’hazemanim (‘Who sanctifies Israel and the seasons’); it is the people of Israel who sanctify the seasons. In the concluding blessing, Mikadesh Yisrael v’roshei chodashim (‘Who sanctifies Israel and the new moons’), it is Israel who sanctifies the new moon. The sages ask (how about) Mikadesh haShabbat v’Yisrael v’roshei chodashim (‘Who sanctifies Shabbat, Israel, and the new moon’)? Peirush: Even if one says that the holiness of Israel and the seasons or the new moon are connected, the holiness of the Sabbath and Israel are two.143Unlike the holidays that are sanctified by the Sanhedrin that announced the date, Shabbat is not dependent on Israel since it occurs every seventh day and is not based on the establishment of the calendar. He answers that they are really one. What is the reason? Shabbat sanctifies and establishes the holidays and the new moons. Israel is the one who sets the actual times for them. Thus, we say (God) ‘Who sanctifies the Sabbath and Israel, who then sanctifies the time for the season and the new moon.
