Peirush - this is what we say: who sanctifies the Sabbath and Israel, who then sanctifies the seasons and the new moons. The Sabbath is set in Heaven, and the festivals are set by a court. The reason they are both mentioned here is that the sanctity of the Sabbath is the reason for the sanctity of Israel, as is stated, “For this is a sign between Me and you throughout the ages, that you may know that I YHVH have consecrated you.” (Ex. 31:13) Therefore, (Shabbat) is mentioned here because it completes the sanctity of Israel, just as the holiness of Israel is mentioned in connection with the holidays without the Sabbath, since Israel establishes the sanctification of the holidays. Sabbath should have been mentioned in conjunction with festivals, but since it is customary to mention the Sabbath without festivals, it seems fit to mention it in the final closing statement (of the blessing). But Moshia Yisrael and Boneh Yerushalaim144The blessing of Birkat HaMazon: however it sounds more like the 14th blessing of the Amidah, “Return in mercy to Jerusalem, Your city, and dwell therein as You have spoken; and rebuild it soon, in our days, as an everlasting structure, and may You speedily establish the throne of David therein. Blessed are You, Adonoy, Builder of Jerusalem.” Since it mentions both the rebuilding of Jerusalem and the establishment of the Davidic house, the rabbis debated whether this blessing should mention both topics in the concluding blessing are not connected to one another, for even though we need salvation in Jerusalem, we also need it outside of Jerusalem and in the diaspora; they are needed, and therefore we need to conclude blessings. And if you say the blessing ending, “Who chose the Torah, the servant Moses, the people Israel, and prophets of truth and justice,” it concludes with four phrases!145The is one of the concluding blessings for the recitation of the Haftorah. One could answer that these are all one thing; we thank God for Torah, which God gave through Moses, to chastise his people.
All Israel (men) are obligated for all commandments stated in the Torah, whether they are positive or negative commandments.

The reason women are exempt from time-triggered positive commandments is that a woman is subjugated to her husband fo rthe fulfillment of his needs. If she were obligated to perform time-triggered commandments, it might happen that just when she is performing the commandment her husband will command her to do his bidding. If she were to fulfill the command of the Creator and ignores his [her husband's] command, woe to her from her husband! And if she were to fulfill his command and ignore that of the Creator, woe to her from her Maker! Therefore the creator exempted her from his commandments, so that she can be at peace with her husband.

Some are exempt from all mitzvot, such as a deaf-mute (cheresh), a lunatic (shoteh), and a minor. Some are exempt for a limited time, such as a person who is sick, who is engaged in performing another mitzvah, or a blind person. A sick person who is not able to concentrate (li-kavein) is exempt from mitzvot that demand kavanah.161Sefaria: Kavanah is the word for the focused mindset recommended for prayer, i.e. of being before God and of what one is saying. While Jewish Law recognizes the legitimacy of prayer with minimal awareness, it requires knowledge of what one is saying in the first blessing of the Amidah. If one’s illness grows more serious, according to the severity of the illness, one is exempt. The Mishnah teaches, “The ill and their caretakers are exempt from the mitzvah of sukkah.162Mishnah Sukkah 2:4 When one is engaged in performing a mitzvah, one is exempt from a mitzvah. It is taught in the Mishnah: “A groom is exempt from reciting Shema on the first night (of marriage).”163Mishnah Berachot 2:5 It is taught in a braita, “Rabbi Yaakov said, ‘Concerning scribes of Torah scrolls, phylacteries, and mezuzot, the merchants who sell them, and the merchants who purchase them from the other merchants and sells them to others, and all who are engaged in the labor of Heaven, including the sellers of the sky-blue dye for ritual fringes, are exempt from reciting Shema, reciting the Amidah prayer, donning phylacteries and all mitzvot that are mentioned in the Torah”164BT Sukkot 26a. In the Talmud the statement is attributed to Rabbi Hannanya ben Akavya Similarly, (this is the law for) one whose deceased relative is laid out unburied before him, one who watches over the deceased, and a blind person. It is also taught in Baba Kama, Ch. 8, (Perek Hachovel): “Rabbi Judah says, ‘A blind person does not receive compensation for humiliation, and, similarly, Rabbi Yehuda exempted a blind person from all mitzvot stated in the Torah... What is the reasoning of Rabbi Yehuda? The verse states: “And this is the commandment, statutes, and laws” (Deut. 6:1), to teach that anyone subject to civil laws (mishpatim) is also subject to the commandments (mitzvot) and statutes (chukim), and anyone who is not subject to civil laws, is also not subject to the commandments and statutes.’”165BT Baba Kamma 87a We say in the first chapter of Kiddushin, “Rav Yosef, who was blind, said: At first I would say: If someone would tell me that the halakha is according with Rabbi Yehuda, who says: A blind person is exempt from the mitzvot, I would make a festive day for the rabbis, as I am not commanded and yet I perform the mitzvot. This means my reward is very great. Now that I have heard that which Rabbi Ḥanina says: Greater is the one who is commanded and performs it than one who is not commanded and performs it, on the contrary: If someone would tell me that the halakha is not in accordance with Rabbi Yehuda, and a blind person is obligated in mitzvot, I would make a festive day for the rabbis.”166BT Kiddushin 31a And if you were to ask, what is the explanation for this? Shouldn’t the one who is not obligated but chooses to observe mitzvot be considered greater, even though this one is not obligated, he observes mitzvot! One could answer that the one who is commanded worries constantly and tries harder to observe the commandments; the one who is not commanded does not worry, but if the opportunity comes along, he will do it, and if not, he doesn’t do it! It is taught. “According to the trouble is the reward.”167Pirkei Avot 5:23 Or else (one might say), since the one who is commanded is punished if he doesn’t observe the mitzvah, it makes sense that the one who then observes it receives an even greater reward. But the one who is not commanded, since he is not punished he also does not receive such a great reward

Rambam OB” M writes that women, slaves, and minors are exempt from wearing fringes according to Torah law.168Rambam, Mishneh Torah, Tzitzit 3:9 From the words of the sages (we learn) that a minor who can wrap himself is obligated to wear tzitzit so that he will learn to follow the mitzvot. Women and slaves who want to wear fringes may do so without (reciting) a blessing; the same is true for other positive commandments from which women are exempt. They may observe them without reciting a blessing, and we do not prevent them. The Ra’avad disagrees with the Rambam, and this is what he says. Avraham (Ra’avad) says, ‘This is the law specifically in the case of fringes that do not contain ke’layim.169While tzitzit may contain shatnez (a mixture of wool and linen), they may not wear them since they are bound by the negative mitzvah against shatnez. Kela’yim is the prohibitions in halachah which proscribe the planting of certain mixtures of seeds, grafting, the mixing of plants in vineyards, the crossbreeding of animals, the formation of a team in which different kinds of animals work together, and shatnez, the mixing of wool with linen in garments. (Wikipedia) He also disagreed about reciting a blessing (when wearing tzitzit) since the blessing is also permission (reshut).170Since the blessing is not an obligatory act they may recite it. He brings support for this opinion from Rav Yosef who said, “At first I would say: If someone would tell me that the law is according to Rabbi Yehuda, who says: If a blind person is exempt from mitzvot, I would make a festive day for the rabbis, as I am not commanded and yet I can perform a mitzvah….”171BT Kiddushin 31a This implies that even though one is exempt from mitzvot one can perform them. But if one is not obligated (to perform a mitzvah), it should be prohibited to recite a blessing! If so, then one who performs a forbidden act when saying a blessing over it.172This implies that since it is not forbidden for a woman to perform the mitzvah, it is also not forbidden for her to recite the blessing over it. One is only forbidden to recite the blessing over an act that is forbidden - and in this case a woman may chose to wear a tallit. End quote.
Rabbeinu Tam concurs - Women may recite a blessing for positive time-bound commandments even though they are exempt from them. They may do so even if it is a rabbinic commandment, as in Berachot, Ch. 3 (Mi sh’meito) concerning women being obligated to recite Kiddush by Torah law. There is no concern here regarding, “You shall not take the name of YHVH your God in vain,” (Ex. 20:7). This is not an ‘unnecessary blessing’ since the verse is merely an asmachta, (support).173And not an actual prohibition. In Talmudical hermeneutics, asmachta is an allusion found in the Hebrew Bible for rabbinic prohibitions or any other Halakha. It's an exception in the talmudical hermeneutics, since it doesn't base the law on the cited verse, but uses the verse as a hint. For we learn in Berachot, Ch. 3, (Mi shemeito), if one is unsure whether or not one recited the Shema, one should go back and recite it again and we do not prohibit one from repeating it because of, “You shall not take the name of YHVH in vain,” (Ex 20:7). Since the person intends to perform the mitzvah when they recite the blessing, there is no concern of them transgressing, "Do not take God’s name in vain.” As we have said, we bring proof from the case of the blind person.174BT Berachot 21a Further, a proof is brought from Ch. 10 of Eiruvin, “Michal, daughter of Kushi, (King Saul) would don phylacteries, and the Sages did not protest against her behavior, similar to the opinion of Rabbi Yosi who said that women may place their hands on the head of an offering (before it was offered) even though it is reshut. But Rabbi Yehudah disagreed and said the (sages) should protest…”175BT BT Rosh Hashanah 33a It is taught in a baraita: “Speak to the children of Israel…and he shall place his hands upon the head of the burnt-offering” (Lev. 1:2–4). The phrase “children of Israel” literally means sons of Israel, and this teaches that the sons of Israel place their hands upon offerings, but the daughters of Israel do not place their hands upon offerings; this is the statement of Rabbi Yehuda. Rabbi Yosei and Rabbi Shimon say: It is optional for women to place their hands on the head of an offering before it is slaughtered… It makes sense to say that they protested because she recited a blessing (and not because they performed the act). From this, we may conclude that according to Rabbi Yossi, one may recite a blessing. Further, they brought a proof in Pesachim Ch. 10 (Arvei Pesachim). “Rabbi Acha said, ‘A blind person is exempted from reciting the Haggadah…. Is that so? Didn’t Ravina ask the sages in the house of Rav Sheshet176Rav Sheshet and Rav Yosef were both blind. (who was blind): ‘Who recited the Haggadah in the house of Rav Sheshet?’ They answered him: In the house of Rav Sheshet, Rav Sheshet recited it and the house of Rav Yosef, Rav Yosef recited it…”177BT Pesachim 116b Either Abudraham’s text was different from ours or there is an error here since he attributes this statement to Merimar instead of Ravina They only proved there regarding whether one could fulfill the obligations of others. But when reciting a blessing for oneself, there was no question, even if the blessing is, “Who redeemed us.”178Since this blessing is for the group one might have thought that the blind person could not recite it for others.
The Rosh writes, “This is not a very good proof….for who is asking? Also, the expression Asher Ga’alanu (‘Who redeemed us’) is not referring to a mitzvah blessing since this berachah doesn’t say ‘who commanded us’ and there is no Torah or rabbinic obligation. Also, it seems that there is no proof here because although a blind person is exempt from the Torah, they are obligated by the sages, as is proven in Pesachim Ch. 10 (Arvei Pesachim), where we learn that according to Rav Sheshet and Rav Yosef, matzah at this time is considered a rabbinic obligation. Therefore, they were able to recite the blessing and say, ‘Who commanded us,’ just as we say in the case of the Chanukah lights and other rabbinic mitzvot.” The reason we obligate the blind man rabbinically, while women are exempt, is that men fall into the category of those who are normally obligated. Also, a man should not appear like a non-Jew who does not observe the Torah, while women are obligated to perform all the non-time-bound mitzvot as well as negative commandments. This ends the Rosh’s comments. Rabbi Yitzchak ben Giat brings a proof that women may recite a blessing for time-bound commandments. How do we know this? Everyone is counted in the seven who are called to the Torah, even women and minors, even though women are not commanded to engage in Torah study, as we have written above.
Rabbeinu Tam writes that this is not a proof because the blessings which come before and after the reading of Torah are not designated for Torah Study. Even if one has recited V’haarev na (‘God, make your words of Torah pleasant’) or one has exempted oneself by reciting Ahavah Rabbah179Both of these passages are for the study of Torah in the morning service. must still recite the blessing for the reading of Torah. Also, we know that if there is no Levi, a Kohen may repeat the blessing, even though he just said it. Also when a woman or a child is called to the Torah among the seven aliyot, they are called during the middle readings and not the first or last readings. For in Megillah, Chap. 3 (HaKorei), the first one opens with a blessing and the last one closes with a blessing (and no blessings were said in between.180BT See Megillah 23a and 21a

When reciting a blessing, whether it is a mitzvah blessing or a blessing of enjoyment181Birchot Hanehenin or Birkot Hanaah (“Blessings of Enjoyment”) are blessings of gratitude recited over things given to us by the world, from which we derive pleasure. one should not create an interruption between the blessing and the thing on which one is blessing is said. If one causes an interruption, one must repeat the blessing. However, if one interrupts with words that have to do with the subject of the blessing one need not go back and repeat the blessing as we say regarding the blessing over bread, “One who broke bread, and before eating it, offered a piece to another, and said: “Take it and recite a blessing, take it and recite a blessing, need not recite the blessing again,”182BT Berachot 40a and in similar cases. The Rosh writes that if one slaughters livestock or fowl and afterward says, “Bring others to slaughter,” or if they mention any other matter related to the ritual slaughter, it is not considered an interruption.183Rosh 6:22 Further, the Rosh writes, some say that one who searches for chametz should not speak until completing the search. Some add, if one converses in matters that are not related to the search, one must go back and repeat the blessing. This does not seem right to me. Rather, one should be careful not to speak between the blessing and the search, but once one begins the search, speaking is not considered an interruption. It is just like sitting in a sukkah or conversing during a meal; they are not an interruption, making one go back and recite the blessing for the sukkah, or reciting the blessing over the bread. We only consider conversation an interruption between (arm) tefillin and (head) tefillin, since the first blessing counts for the head tefillin, so that if one talks (after the first blessing), then one has to recite the blessing lihaniach tefillin, “for the placing of tefillin,” again, according to Rabbeinu Tam. According to Rashi, however, they are considered two mitzvot; they do not prevent one another. Even if one does not converse, one still recites the blessing, Al Mitzvat tefillin, “Concerning the mitzvah of tefillin (when putting on head tefillin). Therefore, there can be an interruption (between the two tefillins). Still, in the first place, it is better to be careful not to engage in needless conversation until one completes the search in order to concentrate during the entire search for chametz and search properly in all the rooms and attics, and any place where chametz may be found.

Rabbi Yaakov ben HaRosh writes: A person must be intentional about the meaning of the words in the blessings one recites. When one mentions God’s name,184Abudraham is referring to YHVH, the tetragrammaton. While it is pronounced Adonai, it is written Yud Hay Vav Hay. one simultaneously focuses on the pronounced word, Adonai, spelled aleph dalet vav nun yud, which is the language of sovereignty. But one should also focus on the written name of God, whose pronunciation is unknown, spelled Yud Hay Vav Hay. According to tradition, this name was only pronounced by the high priest once a year in the Holy of Holies. This is the language of existence, since God “was, is, and will be.” When one says elohim, one should focus on God’s power and might; that God is all powerful among those above and below. El is the language of strength and power as in, “God carried away the nobles of the land.” (Ez. 17:13)

We read in Menachot, Ch. 4 (Perek HaTechlet): “It is taught in a Braita. Rabbi Meir said, ‘A person is obligated to recite 100 blessings every day, as is written, “And now, Israel, what [ma] does the Lord your God require of you” (Deut 10:12). Do not read it as Ma (what) but Meah (100).185BT Menachot 43b You will find that if you switch the letters according to At Bash186The Atbash cipher is a particular type of monoalphabetic cipher formed by taking the alphabet and mapping it to its reverse, so that the first letter becomes the last letter, the second letter becomes the next to last letter, and so on. Atbash - Wikipedia equals 100; י"ם ה"ץ Mem switches with a yud (10) and hay switches with a tzadi (90). There is also a hint from the prophets, as is written, “What does the Lord require of you (mimcha) ” (Micah 6:8). The numerical value of mimcha, “from you,” is 100. There is also an allusion to this in the Writings (Ketuvim), as is stated, “So shall (ki khayn) the person who fears YHVH be blessed.” (Ps. 128:4) The numerical value of Ki khayn, “So shall” shall a person bless is 100. These are the 100 blessings that are recited either during the day or night:
1. Al nitilat yadaim - washing the hands
2. Asher yatzar - upon exiting the privy
3. Elohai neshama - for returning our soul
4. Hanoten lisechvi - gave the rooster understanding
5. Pokeah ivrim - gave sight to the blind
6. Matir asurim - who frees the bound
7. Malbish Arumim - who dresses the naked
8. Zokef kefufim - strengthens the bowed down
9. Magbiah Shefalim - raises the lowly
10. Roka ha’aretz - spreads the earth above the waters
11. Sha’asa li tzorchi - provides our needs
12. Ozer Yisrael Begevurah - Girds Israel with might
13. Hameichin mitzadei - who prepares a person’s steps
14. Shlo asani goy - did not make me a gentile
15. Shlo asani aved - who did not make me a slave
16. Shlo asani esha - did not make me a woman
17. Hamavir sheina - removes sleep from my eyes
18. Al divrei torah - blessings for torah study
19. Ha’arev na - blessings for torah study
20. Asher Bachar Banu - blessing for torah study
21. Tzitzit - wearing a tallit or fringes
22. Tefillin - wearing phylacteries
23. Baruch Sh’amar - opening blessing for zemirot.
This adds up to twenty-three blessings
24. 8 blessings morning and evening before and after the Shema - 3 in the morning and 4 at night, plus yeru einenu - recited by some in evening service
32. 19 blessings, including the blessing against sectarians - it is recited three times a day. These are three recitations of the Amida, which add up to 57 blessings. Together with the previous blessing, this adds up to eighty-eight blessings
89. 12 blessing at meals - six at each meal: one for washing. One for motzi. Four blessings in Grace after meals. This adds up to 100 blessings, not including the blessing for wine, fruit…
On Sabbath and holy days, one lacks 38 blessings since the Tefillah prayer of Sabbath and holidays only has seven blessings in each of its recitations. There are 19 blessings in the weekday Amidah; one is lacking 12 blessings in each Amidah prayer, which adds up to 36 blessings (that are lacking). In addition the blessing for tefillin and the blessing yiru eineinu187Appears before the Amidah in evening service in the Ashkenazic tradition in the diaspora. It generally does not appear in the Sephardic or Edot HaMizrach version of the evening prayers and generally is not recited in the land of Israel. adding up to 38 blessings. How does one make up for these blessings on the Sabbath and holidays? One recites one blessing that includes all 7 (in the evening service) and Kiddush at home. There are 7 blessings in the Musaf Amidah. Together, this adds up to 9 blessings. At the third meal on the Sabbath, there are 6 blessings (washing, motzi, and Birkat Hamazon of which there are 4 blessings. Together they add up to 15 blessings. We are still lacking 23 blessings. One would add blessings for wine and water, and read in Menachot, Ch. 4 (Perek HaTechelet) Rav Ḥiyya, son of Rav Avya, said, “ On Shabbat and Festivals, when there were not enough blessings, they made an effort to fill this quota of blessings with blessings be’isparmakei and migdamei.”188BT Menachot 43b Peirush: be’isparmakei were spices, and migdamei were sweet fruits. How did they do so? They would make spice, and on one of them, they would say a particular blessing, and on another, for spice, they would say a blessing that was fitting for each one. One would then eat a small amount of greens, and one would recite a blessing before and after it, and then one would eat some fruit and recite the blessing before and after it, counting all the blessings until they added up to 100 blessings. One would also have the intention on the Sabbath and holidays to listen to the blessings for the Torah and Haftorah and answer Amen after them, for the sage said that the one who answers Amen is greater than the one who recites the blessing.189BT Berachot 53b (In this way) The blessings add up to 1oo, and if one can add even more blessings, it is praiseworthy, as David said, “As for me, I will hope always, and add to the many praises of You.” (Ps. 71:14) And he also said, “My mouth counts Your blessings, of Your deliverance all day long, though I know not how to count them.” (Ps. 71:15)190I have translated this verse in the way that I believe Abudraham is reading it, based on the homoletical reading of the verse and not on the literal meaning of the verse. The Hebrew verb יספר SFR can mean to tell or to count.
text.4_Weekday Prayers, 0_Bedtime Recitation: I will now explain, with God’s help, the order of blessings and prayers (we recite) with the help of the One enthroned on praises, who instructs people with insight.1 The expressions, “Enthroned on praises,” and “Who instructs people with insight,” are taken from Psalms 22:5 and 94:10

One who gets into bed at night to sleep recites, Blessed…Who makes the bands of sleep fall upon my eyes and slumber upon my eyelids,2BT Berachot 60b, Mishnah Torah, Prayer and Priestly Blessings 7:1, Shulchan Aruch, Orech Chaim 239 is based on the verse, “Give no sleep to your eyes nor slumber to your eyelids.” (Pro. 6:4). “One who makes bands of sleep,” (hevlei sheina) is based on, “The portions (havalim) have fallen unto me in pleasant places, etc,” (Ps. 16:6) followed by, “I bless YHVH who guides me; my conscience admonishes me at night.” (Ps. 16:7)3While the word havalim appears both in the blessing and in Psalms, the connection between the two is not at all clear. Abudraham connects the use of the word havalim to the following verse which states “My conscience admonishes me at night.” Possibly sleep is viewed as a region not only of rest but judgment, as a separate region of being. Hevlei sheina (bands of sleep) is explained as portions of the periods of sleep. Some explain that hevlei sheina is similar to hevlei yoleida (the pangs of childbirth). When a person is unable to sleep for a long time, hevlei sheina, pangs of agony, overtake them, as stated in Nedarim: “ if one takes an oath not to sleep for three days, the court flogs the person, and they are made to sleep immediately.”4BT Nedarim 15a, language slightly different We make a blessing for sleep because it is a basic human need, as is stated in Bereshit Rabbah: “Rabbi Shimon ben Elazar said: 'And behold it was very good' – and behold sleep is good. Is sleep, then, very good? Did we not learn: Wine with sleep is beneficial for the wicked and beneficial for the whole world? However, as a result of a person sleeping a bit, he can get up and toil extensively in the Torah.”5Bereshit Rabbah 9:6, BT Sanhedrin 71a When the wicked are sleeping or under the influence of wine, they are less likely to do harm to others or to the world “One who illuminates the pupil of my eye” is based on “Guarded him like the pupil of His eye.” (Deut. 32:10) It states that when a person desires to sleep, the pupil of their eye grows dark, and when one sleeps and wakes up, the pupil of one’s eyes brightens.

May it be Your will, Adonai, my God and God of my ancestors, to make me lie down in peace, is based on the verse, “Safe and sound, I lie down and sleep.” (Ps. 4:9). And that You raise me up for life and for peace. These two expressions are meant to include the preservation of the soul and the body. “For life” refers to the soul, because when one sleeps, one is like a corpse, and one’s soul is in the hands of the Holy One, and it is then returned in the morning, as if one is being brought back to life. “For peace” refers to the body, because at night one encounters more destructive forces and evil occurrences than during the day; so, a person prays that one might remain bodily whole. Let neither bad dreams nor troubling thoughts disturb me. That is, I should not have sinful thoughts even in my dreams and let my bed be perfect before You.6Literally the expression is “My bed is complete” See Shir HaShirim Rabbah 3:7, Bereshit Rabbah 76:1 Peirush:7Note that the comments beginning Peirush - are not part of the talmudic text but the author’s explanations.If one engages in intimate relations with one's spouse, the offspring that will emerge will be complete in the service of God, and I will not give birth to unworthy seed. This is what the Sage OB'M said about Jacob. His bed was complete since he did not give birth to unfit offspring. But unfit children were found among Abraham’s and Isaac’s offspring. And illumine my eyes lest I sleep a sleep of death. In other words, return my soul to me so that my sleep is not eternal sleep. Blessed are You, Adonai, who illuminates the whole world in His glory. Raise them from their beds into the light of day so they can go about their tasks.

One recites the first paragraph of the Sh’ma. For we read in Berachot, Ch. 9 (HaRoeh), “One who enters to sleep on his bed recites from Shema Yisrael (Deut. 6:4) until Vehaya im shamoa. (Deut. 11:13) Rabbeinu Hananel writes that one must also recite Vehaya im shamoa, since it contains the phrase “When you lie down and when you rise up.” (Deut. 11:19) The Rosh writes, it is possible that Rabbeinu Hananel recited Shema Yisrael, Vahaya im shamoa, and Yoshev b’seter elyon, “You who dwell in the shelter on high,” (Ps. 91) up to “Because you made YHVH my refuge,” (Ps. 91:9) since there are sixty words up to the word, mahsi מַחְסִ֑י (my refuge). There are 60 letters in the Priestly Benediction. Regarding them (the letters), it is stated, “There is Solomon’s couch, encircled by sixty warriors.” (Song 3:7) This refers to the Holy Temple. The warriors are the letters of the Priestly Benediction, “All of them, holding a sword,” (Song 3:8) The Sages OB'M, said, all of these verses (of the Priestly Benediction) mention the name of God (YHVH) “May YHVH bless you,” “May YHVH shine upon you,” “May YHVH lift up His Face upon you,” (Nu. 6:25-27) One recites, “A psalm of David when he fled from his son Absalom. YHVH, my foes are so many,” (Ps. 3:1-2) until, “Deliverance is YHVH’s; Your blessing be upon Your people! Selah.” (Ps. 3:9) One also recites Hashkeevaynu (“Let us lie down”) until, “Guard our going out and our coming in forever,” but one does not recite a concluding blessing. One recites, “Blessed is HaShem by day, Blessed is Hashem by night. Blessed is HaShem when we lie down. Blessed is HaShem when we rise. In Your hands are the souls of the living and the dead. In His hand is every living soul and the breath of all humanity. (Job 12:10) Into Your hand I entrust my spirit; You redeem me, Hashem, faithful God. (Ps. 31:6) One says, HaShem said to Satan… (Zech. 3:2)8The full verse is, “But [the angel of] YHVH said to the Accuser, “YHVH rebuke you, O Accuser; may YHVH who has chosen Jerusalem rebuke you! For this is a brand plucked from the fire.” One says, “When you lie down you will not be afraid.” (Pro. 3:2) “The Lord will guard your going out and coming in.” (Ps. 121:8) “There is Solomon’s couch, encircled by sixty warriors. All of them, carrying swords. ” (Song 3:7) “HaShem will bless you and guard you, until “And grant you peace. They should immediately go to sleep.

Rabbi Hai Gaon writes that it is fitting to place the blessing before the Shema, Psalms, and all these verses so that one can fall asleep while reciting them. He brings a proof from the Jerusalem Talmud which says: “Rabbi Zeira read the Shema over and over again until he drifted off to sleep.”9JT Berachot 1:1 It is interesting to note that Abudraham does not actually quote the text of the Talmud but alludes to it. It is possible that he did 'not have the text in front of him and he is referring to this text from memory. The Sages state, in Ch. 1 of Berachot, “Rabbi (Elazar) said: Anyone who recites Shema while in bed, it is as if he holds a double-edged sword, as it is stated: “Let the faithful exult in glory; let them sing for joy upon their beds. Praises of God in their mouths, and a double-edged sword in their hands” (Ps. 149:6). Peirush: “Let them sing for joy upon their beds,” means one should rejoice when reciting matters related to retiring, as in, “When you lie down.” (Deut 6:8) Rabbi Yitzḥak said: Anyone who recites Shema while in bed, demons stay away from him. As it is stated: “And the sparks [reshef] fly [uf] upward” (Job 5:7). The word “sparks” means demons, as it is stated: “Wasting of hunger, and the devouring of the sparks [reshef] and bitter destruction [ketev meriri]” (Deut. 32:24). The word fly [uf]means Torah, as it is stated: “Will you set your eyes upon it? It is gone.” (Pr. 23:5)10BT Berachot 5a The Talmudic text is presented in a slightly different order The Hidushei Devash11 Chiddushei Devash was written by David ben Saul of Narbonne who lived in the thirteenth century in Provence. Leor Jacobi: Talmudic "Honey", Fragments of the Novellae of R. David ben Saul of Narbonne states, Some do not read the text, “The word fly (uf) means Torah, as it is stated: “Will you set your eyes upon it? It is gone.” (Pr. 23:5) Rather, it (should be), “The word fly (uf) only means the Shema, for it is stated, 'One repeats it (the Shema) twice, once in the daytime and once at night, and Uf also means double, like the word V’khafalta “When you fold over,” (Ex. 26:9)12“Join five of the cloths by themselves, and the other six cloths by themselves; and fold over (v’khafalta) the sixth cloth at the front of the tent.” In the Aramaic translation of the Torah, the word v’khaaflata is translated as vtei’uf, from the same word, Uf. Since the curtain is doubled over. which is translated וְתֵיעוּף v’tei’uf in the Targum. And if you were to challenge this by saying, "If so, one should also be required to say the Amidah twice!" One could retort that the number of times one recites the Amidah is rabbinic (and not a Torah requirement like the Shema). Also, the Amidah is not recited twice but three times. Some people, when they recite the Shema before going to bed, recite the blessing, “Praised are you Adonai, our God, Eternal Sovereign, who sanctified us with the commandments and commanded us to accept upon ourselves the Sovereignty of Heaven with a complete heart.” They are mistaken because the Shema, which is recited in synagogue, is the essential one, since it is recited along with its blessings. This (Shema) is only optional, as we explained above.
text.4_Weekday Prayers, 1_Morning Blessings,:
It is written in Machzor Vitri,13Simhah ben Samuel of Vitry (died 1105) was a French Talmudist of the 11th and 12th centuries, pupil of Rashi, and the compiler of Machzor Vitry. Simhah ben Samuel of Vitry - Wikipedia “One who wakes at midnight to study Torah should wash his hands and recite the blessing, Al Netilat Yadaim, ‘Concerning the washing of hands.” If one relieves oneself, one recites, Asher Yatzar, “Who fashioned humans,” and all the following blessings. One recites the blessings of Torah, and then one says, Ezehu mikoman (“Where are the offerings sacrificed in the Temple,”)14Mishnah Zevachim 5:1-8 These passages deal with the daily sacrifices in the temple as well as the incense offerings. They are often simply referred to as the Korbanot. and Rabbi Yishmael omer (“Rabbi Ishmael taught”)15This passage is a Braita; it is the introduction to the Sifra, a Midrash on Leviticus. It contains 13 hermeneutic principles of interpretation of Jewish law. It appears as an introduction to the laws in the Sifra and as a follow up to the Mishnah as a kind of Talmudic passage so that upon reciting the Torah blessings, we study a portion of the Torah, Mishnah and Gemara.. Upon entering the synagogue, one begins wherever one left off (reciting these blessings and passages). Ibn Yarchi writes that if one wakes to read Torah before sunrise, one should recite the blessings. Still, one does not recite the sacrifice since the sacrifices were only offered in the daytime, as is stated, “On the day God commanded Israel to offer their sacrifices.” (Lev. 7:38) One should only recite the sacrifices at the time when they were offered - end quote.
Similarly, one only recites the blessing, lisechvi bina, “Who gave the rooster understanding,” in the daytime. The Rosh16Rabbi Asher ben Yehiel 1250-1327, known as the Rosh. also states this. If one rises before the time when the Amidah is recited to write words of Torah, one is obligated to recite the blessing over Torah study, provided one writes only about mundane matters (reshut).17For instance, in addition to studying Torah one stops to write a letter to a friend or jot down some personal notes. We read in the first chapter of Berachot, “Rav Huna said that Shmuel said: One who rises to study Torah, before the time of the Shema, one must recite the blessing over Torah study. Once one has recited the Shema (and its blessings), one need not recite the blessing for Torah study. What is the reason? One has already exempted oneself with Ahavah Raba: “With abounding love.”18BT Berachot 11b. JT Berachot 1:5 The quote in the Talmud is stated in the name of Rabbi Yehudah in the name of Samuel. There are other differences in the language. We read in the Jer. Talmud, “Rabbi Abba said, This applies only if one studied Torah immediately (after Ahavah Rabba).”19JT Berachot 1:5 The opinion of the Jer. Talmud is that the benediction before Shema is no substitute for the benediction on Torah study. Rabbi Abba appears to be saying that one is only exempt from reciting the blessing over Torah study if one immediately studies after saying Ahavah Rabbah- this is odd since one usually recites the Shema after Ahavah Rabbah. However the recitation of the shema is technically not Torah story. One possibility (Tiferet Shmuel) suggests that it means that one studies Torah immediately after finishing one’s prayers but there are many other explanations. The Rosh writes that this statement refers to Ahavah Rabba, since it is recited only for a mitzvah of Torah recitation, such as the Shema, and is recited immediately upon learning Torah. In that case, it counts as a mitzvah blessing, and one does not have to recite the Torah-study blessing again that day, even if one pauses and then resumes studying Torah. Similarly, if one recites the blessing for Torah study and learns Torah, one does not have to recite the blessing again if one stops in the middle of the study. That is why it was necessary to say, “Only if one studies Torah immediately after Ahavah rabbah,” but not for the blessing for Torah study. For if one did not make this distinction (between the blessing for Torah study and Ahavah rabbah), one might think that a pause is considered an interruption, and one must go back and repeat the blessing even in the case of Ahavah Rabbah. It makes sense that people who regularly engage in Torah study and quickly return to their studies, even when attending to their daily tasks. They are constantly preoccupied with learning (even when they pause), so that it is not considered a break from learning. Even if they learn Torah at night, the night follows the day, and one does not have to recite the blessing again as long as one has not slept. Anyone who sleeps regularly in bed during the day is considered to have taken a regular break; the person should repeat the blessing—end quote.

It is forbidden to eat or drink in the morning before reciting the Amida prayer, as stated in Berachot, “Rabbi Yosei, son of Rabbi Ḥanina, said in the name of Rabbi Eliezer ben Ya’akov: What is the meaning of the verse: “You shall not eat with the blood” (Leviticus 19:26)? (It means) you may not eat before you pray for your blood (your life). Rabbi Yitzḥak said that Rabbi Yoḥanan said in the name of Rabbi Eliezer ben Ya’akov: One who eats and drinks and before one prays, (and only then accepts the kingdom of heaven), about him the verse states: “And Me you have cast behind your back” (I Kings 14:9). Do not read ‘Your back’ [gavekha]; rather, ‘your arrogance’’ [ge’ekha]. The Holy One, said: One who eats and drinks, and then accepts the kingdom of Heaven is arrogant.”20BT Berachot 10b From here Avi HaEzri21Eliezer ben Joel. Often referred to as the Ra’avya; 1140-1225 See Eliezer ben Joel HaLevi - Wikipedia concludes that it is permissible to drink water in the morning before prayer, since water is not associated with arrogance. The Rif writes that even drinking water is forbidden since it satisfied one’s soul and one’s desire with what it needs after one has become arrogant. The Ri writes that if one begins eating before sunrise, once sunrise occurs one must stop, even though we say regarding the afternoon prayer that if one began eating, one does not have to stop. That is different since that is based on a scriptural allusion, and not eating before Shacharit is based the verse, “You shall not eat with the blood.”22That is, eating in the morning is considered “life saving” so we do not eat until after prayer since we attribute our lives to God. At Minchah, the meal is not considered “life saving,” so the prohibition against eating is not as stringent.

Rabbi Ya’akov ben HaRosh writes, A person should rise in the morning to serve one’s creator, even if one’s inclination taunts him in the winter, saying, “How can you get up when it’s so cold,” or it taunts him in the summer, saying, “How can you get up from your bed when you have not had enough sleep?’ Rather, one should resolve to rise up, for you should awaken the dawn, and it should not awaken you, as King David OB’M said, “Awake, my soul, awake, harp and lyre; I will awaken the dawn,” (Ps. 57:9). ‘I awaken the dawn, but the dawn does not awaken me.’ One should tell oneself, ‘If I were serving a mortal king and he commanded me to rise with the morning light to serve him, I would be careful and zealous to rise to his service as he commanded. How much more so before the King of king of kings, the Holy One of blessing23Tur, Orech Chaim 1:1 1270 - 1340, Rabbi Yaakov ben Asher, the son of the Rosh and the author of the Arba’a Turim. He is often referred to as Ba’al HaTurim or Rabbi Yaakov ben HaRosh. Jacob ben Asher - Wikipedia - end quote.

When one wakes up, if one needs to attend to one’s needs, one says to the accompanying angels, “Be honored, holy honorable ones, servants of the Most High,”24BT Berachot 60b, Rambam Mishneh Torah Laws of Prayer and the Priestly Benedictions 7:5, This statement appears with slight variations. One should do so at a distance of four amot from the lavatory. For we read in Bereshit Rabbah, Rabbi Sheila said, “There are two ministering angels who accompany a person and testify against him, as is stated: 'For He will command His angels over you, to guard you in all your ways”(Ps. 91:11).25BT Haggigah 16a, in the name of Rabbi Zarika. A similar quote appears in Ta’anit in the name “of the school of Rabbi Sheila.”
This refers to different circumstances. If the person is good, one is guarded by them, and if not, the guarding is withdrawn, and the angels testify against one, and they report to the great court. And the person says to the angels: “Lift up your honor for yourselves, for I am not worthy that you should bear honor on my account. Servants of the Most High! That is to say, it is only because of the service of God that you accompany me. Therefore, give honor to the God of Israel.”26There does not appear to be a single source for this idea. However upon consulting ChatGPT I found a number of sources that are similar to it in BB 119b; Rabbinic literature. BT ShaPirkei’D’Rebbe Eliezer 34; Midrash Tanhuma Vayishlach 3; Sefer Hasidim 770; and Zohar II, 94a Pinchas What is the “honor” (the individual is referring to?) “Guard me, guard me, help me, help me…. wait for me, wait for me until I enter and come out, as this is the way of man.”27BT Berachot 60b The Hiddushei Devash28See Footnote 18 above writes that this blessing should only be recited by those who are God fearing and pious, since the Shechinah dwells with them, but other people should not say it because it is considered arrogant. Once one has defecated one should only clean oneself with one's left hand, as we read at the end of Berachot, “Rabbi Akiva said: I once entered the bathroom after my teacher Rabbi Yehoshua, and I learned three things: I learned that one should uncover oneself but rather one should not uncover himself while standing but while sitting;29The word נפרעין, uncovering oneself, is a euphemism for urinating The Jer. Talmud adds, “Only if there is no wall.”30JT Berachot 5:9 Therefore, we are not particular about this since our restrooms have partitions. “I learned that one should not defecate while facing east and west, but while facing north and south.”31BT Berachot 62a. The order of the three teachings is different in Berachot from Abudraham. The quote is broken up in Abudraham in order to add the separate statement from the Jerusalem Talmud. “And I learned that one should not wipe with his right hand, but with his left. Ben Azzai said to him: You were impertinent to your teacher to that extent that you observed that much? He replied: It is Torah, and I must learn.”32BT Berachot Ibid. 62a Why does one clean oneself with the left hand and not the right? Because of the way Torah was given, as is stated, “From his right hand a fiery law went forth for them.” (Deut. 33:2) Rabba bar bar Ḥana said: Because the right hand is close to the mouth. And Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish said: Because one ties the phylacteries onto his left hand with his right hand. Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak said: Because one points to the cantillation notes of the Torah.”33Ibid 62a One shows young children the notes with one’s right hand, as zarka, pazer gadol, and shalshelet. When they read it, they lift and lower their hand to help them understand their reading. One should clean their body with a stone or a garment to remove filth.

When one goes out of the privy one washes one’s hands and recites the blessing, “Praised are You Adonai,” this is based on the verse, “Praised are you Adonai who teaches me Your laws.” (Ps. 119:12) The term baruch is not a passive verb;34 (Pa’ul) In other words it is not a passive expression of one who is blessed by others, but rather it is an expression of one who is a source of blessing. rather like merciful (rachum), and gracious, (chanun), it means that God is the source of all blessings and does not receive a blessing from anyone else. “Our God,” is based on the verse “I am YHVH, your God,” (Ex. 20:2) which the Holy One said, and on the verse, “Hear O Israel, YHVH our God,” (Deut. 6:4) which Israel says. “An everlasting sovereign,” is based on the verse, “An everlasting sovereign.’ (Jer. 10:10) “Who sanctified us with His commandments,” based on, “You shall sanctify yourselves and be holy.” (Lev. 11:44) and on, “To be to Him a holy people and to keep His commandments.”35Grinzeig points out in his commentary that there is no verse exactly like this one. See Numbers 26:18-19 There are some commentators who say that the language here is the language of betrothal and marriage since the Holy One becomes betrothed to Israel through mitzvot, as is stated, “I will betroth you with (emunah) faithfulness,” (Ho. 2:21) and the mitzvot are called faithfulness, as Scripture states, “All Your commandments are faithful.” (Ps. 119:86) “And He commanded us” is based on the verse, “When Moses commanded us to keep the Torah,” (Deut. 33:4) “Ibn Yarchi writes, “I asked regarding the blessing, why is the beginning addressed directly to God as if the speaker is standing before Him (Baruch ata adonai) and the end, as if the speaker is not in God’s presence (melech ha’olam). I found a lovely answer in the midrash based on what is stated, “I am ever mindful of YHVH’s presence.” (Ps. 16:8) When one mentions the name of God and says, “Praised are You, Adonai,” one stands in the presence of God; afterwards, when one says “Eternal sovereign,” it seems as though one is not standing before God, for it is as if one is saying, He is our God who is an everlasting sovereign who sanctified us with His commandments and commanded us to perform them. The Ribach OB’M writes that the reason the Sages decreed that blessings should be in second and third person is because the Holy One is both revealed and hidden. God is revealed from the aspect of His acts and hidden from the aspect of God’s divinity. Similarly, the soul is both apparent and hidden; as a result the blessing is blessed both in the second and the third person, as we say, “Bless YHVH, O my soul, all my being, His holy name.”36Thus, the verse begins in the second person “Bless my soul,” and it concludes in the second person, “His holy name.” The same transition takes place in Psalm 104. Just as God is both revealed and hidden - so too, human beings are revealed (through speech) and hidden (in thought). (Ps. 103:1)
Bless YHVH, O my soul; YHVH, my God, You are very great; You are clothed in glory …” (Ps. 104:1-2) “At your rebuke they fled at Your blast, rushed away at the sound of Your thunder.” 104:7) Blessing is through the speech of the mouth and the thought of the heart — the heart is hidden, but the voice is heard. A human being is composed of body and soul. It would be fitting for him, by virtue of his soul, to cleave to his Creator and stand before Him constantly; however, he cannot do so because of his body. Therefore, his blessings are both directed before [God] and yet hidden. This explanation is more correct than the first.

If you ask, what use are our blessings to the Holy One, one could answer that we recite blessings so that we might be worthy of God’s blessing, as the Sages, OB’M, “One who blesses is blessed.”37See BT Sota 38b through mitzvot that we may give Similarly, Scripture states, “Lift your hands toward the sanctuary and bless YHVH. May YHVH, maker of heaven and earth, bless you from Zion.” (Ps. 134:2-3) The reason for these blessings is that God chose us that He might sanctify us with mitzvot. We also do so that we might give thanks for the food and the other physical enjoyments, that our bodies should be healthy and our souls at ease when thinking of God’s kindnesses, and that we may give thanks to His name.

One says, “Concerning the washing of the hands,” (Al netilat yadaim) using the expression netilah. One does so because the utensil one uses is called a natla, a talmudic expression. Some explain that this word is related to the expression ותשאני רוח ‘lifting up,’‘Then a spirit lifted me up’ (Ez. 3:12), which is translated in the Aramaic as, ונטלתני (unetalatanee). Also, (it is related to the verse), “He raised them, and exalted them, all the days of old.” (Is. 63:9) This is what is stated in the first chapter of Sota, “One who washes his hands must raise one’s hands upward, lest the water advance past the joints (the parts of the hands one is not required to wash) and then return to the area one had washed, rendering one’s hands ritually impure.”38BT Sota 4b There is an allusion to Netilat Yadaim in the Torah: “If one with a discharge does not rinse his hands in water, touches another person, that person shall wash his clothes, bathe in water, and remain unclean until evening.” (Lev. 15:11) The Sages stated that anyone who is neglectful in the washing of hands in the end will be impoverished.39BT Shabbat 62bAn allusion to this is the abbreviation of al netilat yadaim, whose abbreviation is ani, poor.

Afterwards, one says, “Praised are you Adonai, our God, eternal sovereign40Melech haOlam could also be translated “Sovereign of the Universe,” or “Sovereign of the world.” who fashioned human beings.” The rule that an “adjacent blessings”41When blessings follow one another, the second blessing is called a “adjacent blessing,” and it is commonly the practice not to begin the second blessing with Baruch attah… In this case, however, even though Asher yatzar follows the blessing for washing one’s hands, one still begins with Baruch atta. does not apply to this berachah because one recites Al netilat yadaim many times without immediately reciting Asher yatzar. The rule of adjacent blessings only applies where the first blessing begins with Baruch, and these blessings are always juxtaposed, and one does not recite one without the other.42Asher Yatzar must begin with Baruch because it is not always attached to the handwashing blessing. People say al netilat yadaim many times without asher yatzar in between Asher Yatzar is based on the verse, “YHWH, God, fashioned the human.”43The Hebrew word here is Adam. (Gen. 2:7) “With wisdom,” is based on, “YHVH created the earth with wisdom.” (Pro. 3:19) Scripture states, “Have you not poured me out as milk, and curdled me like cheese?” (Job 10:10) because God created humans from a putrid drop44Mishneh Avot 3: and fashioned them with wisdom. “And created openings,” to keep a person alive. God created eyes so one could see with them. God created eyelids so that one can close one’s eyes and sleep and so that one doesn’t have to look at evil, as is stated, “Shuts his eyes against looking at evil.” (Is. 33:15) God created the openings of the ears to hear with them. God makes the openings of the nostrils with which to smell and breathe, and to expel the surplus of moisture from one’s head. God made a mouth for eating and talking, teeth, and incisors to grind the food. God made a tongue to knead the food in one’s mouth and to form words precisely. God made the esophagus and the gullet to swallow food and drink. God created the windpipe to allow the living breath of life to go up and down from the heart, surrounded by the lungs, to the nostrils and the mouth so it could produce the sound of speech from the bronchial passages (symphoni keri’ah). God created the heart to be the dwelling place for the spirit of life and through which one contemplates all one’s thoughts. God created the upper organs, known as the stomach, to digest food and drink, to sustain the body. God made the liver on the right side, with red bile, and the blood in the liver to warm the upper inner organs. And from the heat of the liver and the bile, the food is digested inside the upper organs. God then created the intestines to receive waste from food and drink, and they move it through their twists until it is expelled. God created two kidneys, one on the right and one on the left, to warm the lower stomach, give it life, and help remove waste of all kinds from the body. Further, the Sages state, “The heart understands, and the kidneys advise.”45BT Berachot 61a, Hullin 11a God made the spleen on the left side, together with the black bile, to cool the inner organs, the intestines, the belly, so that the food and drink do not dry out and become ruined because of the boiling heat of the organs, which grow hot and boil from the heat of the blood, the liver, and the red bile. Further, the Sages OB’M say, “The spleens laugh.” God made male and female sexual organs so that humans can reproduce. God made breasts for women so that they may produce milk to suckle infants, bones to give the body a strong structure, and placed muscles on the bones to warm them. He made for him blood vessels, and they descend to provide drink (nourishment) to the entire body through them, running from side to side. He made for him sinews to strengthen the binding of the bones and the limbs. He made for him limbs and joints that are joined together, and the vertebrae of the spine, and the joints of the fingers of the hands and feet, and the arms, thighs, knees, shins, ankles, and soles of the feet, and the vertebrae of the neck and the shoulder-blades of the shoulders—so that he may be able to spread out and bend, to crouch and to straighten up, to stand and to sit, to kneel and to bow, and to turn his head this way and that. He covered him with skin over the flesh, the bones, the sinews, and the nerves, to cover the body so that it would be warm and not become cold, and to protect the body’s moisture and the internal organs. God made the skull to rule over all the limbs, a brain in which reasoning, and where the soul of wisdom dwells. He created moisture around the brain so that the brain and the eyes would not dry out from the heat of the inner organs, which rise from below upward to the head. He made the hair of the head to warm the head so that it should not become cold, since there is no flesh between the skin and the bone of the skull. He made the hairs of the beard because of the beauty and majesty of the face, and so that he would be distinguished in his appearance from women. God made an umbilical cord for males and females to give sustenance (to the fetus) while they are in their mother’s womb until they come out into the world, since the fetus is unable to eat with its mouth because it is closed until it comes into the world. God made hands to feel, to grab, to grasp, to hold on to, and to do the work necessary to live. God created fingernails to distinguish human beings from other creatures and to scratch with them. God created legs so that the body might stand on them and that they might bring it to any place.
Whatever the Holy One created in human beings was made only to serve humans and keep them alive. This is the great wisdom; there is nothing like it. We state in the Sifri, “The Rock, His deeds are perfect.” (Deut. 32:4) “God’s work is whole with all creatures, and His ways are not to be brought into question. The slightest variation is not to be entertained regarding them — "If I had three eyes," "If I had three hands," "If I had three feet," "If I could walk on my head," "If my face faced backwards" — "how wonderful it would be!" This is the intent of "Perfect is His work."46Sifrei Devarim 3017:2

I will now explain the statement of the Sages, OB’M, “If a woman emits seed first, she gives birth to a male, and if a man emits seed first, she gives birth to a female…”47BT Nidah 31a Peirush: This matter is likened as follows: the thing that emerges first is like the earth, and the second thing is the seed, and whatever is sown is what appears. Therefore, when the man emits seed first, he is like the earth, and when the woman’s seed comes afterward, it is the seed, and thus she gives birth to a female.48This is based on a rabbinic, pre-modern, understanding of genetics. It assumes that both men and women emit seed - however, whoever emits it second will cause the gender of the offspring. When the man emits seed first, the gender is determined by the woman and the child is female. If the woman emits seed first, then the sex is determined by the man and the child is male. This is expressed in the Talmudic statement. Earth represents the passive and the seed the active aspect of procreation, thus, whichever one emerges second determines the child’s sex. Likewise, when the woman emits seed first, she gives birth to a male. It is stated in the Jer. Talmud and Vayikra Rabbah, “This is analogous to two painters, this one painted the image of that one, and that one painted the image of this one. The female is always from the man, and the male is always from the woman.” “Rabbi Avin said: There is no barber who trims his own beard. One achieves nothing until another comes and trims it for him. And similarly, it is known that from the seed of the woman comes a female, and from the seed of the man comes a male. However, the one who emits seed first is of no consequence, since the later seed nullifies the earlier one.”49See Vayikra Rabbah 14:9 There does not appear to be a similar source in the Jerusalem Talmud. Ramban OB’M writes, “The intent of the sages was not that the child is formed from the woman’s seed, for although the woman has generative organs [i.e., ovaries] like those of the man, either the seed is not formed by them at all, or [if formed], the seed is not thick and does not contribute anything to the embryo. Rather, the Sages used the term “she emits seed” (tazria) with reference to the blood of the womb, which gathers in the mother at the time of the consummation of coitus, and attaches itself to the seed of the male. For in the opinion of the Rabbis, a child is formed from the blood of the female and the white [semen] of the man, and both of them are called “seed.”50See Ramban Lev. 12:2 Similarly, the Sages state: “There are three partners in [the formation of] a human. The male emits the white [semen], from which are formed the sinews, the bones, and the white substance in the eye. The female emits a red secretion from which are formed skin, flesh, blood, hair, and dark substance in the eye.”51BT Niddah 31a quoted by Ramban In the opinion of the Greek philosophers, however, the whole body of the child is formed from [the substance of] the blood of the mother, the father only contributing that generative force which is known in their language as hyly, which gives form to matter. For there is no difference between the egg of a chicken which is laid because a male fructified it, and that laid as a result of the mother rolling herself in the dust, except that the egg [that was fructified by a male] germinates into a young bird. At the same time, the other is not sown nor beareth, because it is deprived of the elemental heat which is its hyly —end quote.

We read in Niddah Ch. 3 (HaMapelet): Rabbi Samlai taught: To what is a fetus womb comparable? To a folded notebook [lefinkas]. And it rests with its hands on its two sides of its head, at the temples, its two arms on its knees, and its heels on its two buttocks, and its head rests between its knees, and its mouth is closed, but its umbilicus is open. It eats what its mother eats, and drinks from what its mother drinks, and it does not emit excrement lest it kill its mother. Peirush:Therefore, the opening for excrement is closed; also, the fetus does not produce refuse, but urinates as necessary.52BT Niddah 30b So writes Rabbeinu Shmuel ben Hofni.53Samuel ben Hofni, "the Rashbaḥ," died 1034; He was the gaon of Sura Academy in Mesopotamia from 998 to 1012 “But once it emerges into the airspace of the world, the closed limb (mouth) opens, and the open limb (umbilicus) closes; otherwise it could not live for even an hour.”54BT Niddah IBID. We read there, “The Sages taught: ‘During the first three months of pregnancy, the fetus resides in the lower compartment of the womb; in the middle three months, the fetus resides in a middle compartment; and during the last three months of pregnancy, the fetus resides in the upper compartment. Once it's time to emerge, it turns upside down and emerges, causing labor pains. It has been taught: “The labor pains experienced by one who gives birth to a female are greater than those experienced by one who gives birth to a male.”55BT Niddah 31a What is the reason? “This one (a male fetus) emerges in the manner in which it engages in intercourse (facing downward). And that one (a female fetus) emerges in the manner in which it engages in intercourse (facing upward). Consequently, the female turns its face around before it is born, but the male does not turn its face around before it is born. The Sages taught: During the first three months of pregnancy, sexual intercourse is difficult and harmful for the woman and is also difficult for the offspring.” Peirush: Because the fetus dwells in the lower compartment. “During the middle three months, intercourse is difficult for the woman but is beneficial for the offspring.” Rashi writes, “I do not know why. “During the last three months, sexual intercourse is beneficial for the woman and for the offspring; as a result of it, the offspring is found to be strong (miluban) and fair-skinned (mizoraz).56IBID. Meluban means that the seed ‘whitens’ (i.e., completes or perfects) the fetus from its unformed state. And mezoraz means strong and healthy. And Rabbi Saadia writes in the name of the sages of empirical knowledge57The Hebrew expression here is chachmei nisayon. It refers to scientists who come to their conclusions based on experiments and observation rather than theory and pure logic does not. that the place where the fetus dwells in the seventh month is spacious, and in the eighth month it is narrow, and in the ninth month it is widest. Therefore, a child born in the seventh or ninth month lives, but not one born in the eighth month. And it is not unlikely that the place of its entrance and exit is wide, and the area between them is narrow; therefore, one does not circumcise an eight-month-old infant on Shabbat - end quote.

The Sages taught: At first, people would say, if the woman emits seed first, she gives birth to a male, and if the man emits seed first, she gives birth to a female. But the Sages did not explain from where this was derived, until Rabbi Tzadok came and explained that it is derived from the verse: “These are the sons of Leah, whom she bore to Jacob in Paddan Aram, with his daughter Dinah” (Gen. 46:15). The verse attributes the male children to females, as the males are called: The sons of Leah, and the female infants to the males. Scripture states, “And the sons of Ulam were mighty men of valor, archers, and had many sons and sons’ sons” (I Chr. 8:40). Is it in a person’s power to have many sons and sons’ sons? Instead, because they delay while in their wives’ abdomens, initially refraining from emitting semen so that their wives emitted seed first, their children were male, as the verse ascribes them credit as though they have many sons and sons’ sons. This statement is the same as that of Rav Ketina: I could have made all my children male by refraining from emitting seed until my wife emitted seed first. Rava says another method through which one can cause his children to be males: One who wishes to make all of his children males should engage in intercourse with his wife and repeat the act.58BT Niddah 31a-b Peirush: As a result of the initial passion of intercourse, one (person) emits seed first.
It is written in the Book of Conception (Sefer ha-Toledot) that a woman has seven openings: three on the right, three on the left, and one in the middle. If the seed enters those on the right, she will bear a male; if it enters those on the left, she will bear a female; and if it enters the middle, she bears a tumtum or an androgynos. And when she lies on her right side, the seed enters those of the right side, and she bears a male, and the impurity hastens to leave; therefore, she is impure only seven days, and her period of purity is 33 days. When she lies on her left side, she bears a female, and the impurity does not hasten to leave; therefore, she is impure for two weeks, and her period of purity is 66 days. And the Ramban explained that since the nature of the female is cold and moist, and the moisture in the mother’s womb is very great and cold, therefore, a female is born. And for this reason, she requires greater cleansing, because of the abundance of moisture and the stale blood in it; and because of their coldness, it is known that ailments require a longer time for cleansing than those that are hot.

We read in Nidah Ch. 3, (Hamapelet): “The Sages taught: There are three partners in the creation of a person: The Holy One, Blessed be He, and his father, and his mother. His father emits the white seed, from which form the bones, the sinews, the nails, the brain that is in its head, and the white of the eye. His mother emits red seed, from which the skin, the flesh, the hair, and the black of the eye are formed. And the Holy One inserts into him a spirit, a soul, his countenance [ukelaster]” - Peirush: this means splendor of the face - eyesight. Peirush: the eye is created by the mother and father, but it cannot see; we know this because a corpse has eyes and ears, yet it cannot see, hear, or speak. “The hearing of the ear, the capability of speech, the ability of walking with the legs, understanding, and wisdom are God-given. ”And when a person’s time to depart from the world arrives, the Holy One retrieves His part, and leaves the part of the father and mother before them. Rav Pappa said: This is what people say: When you remove the salt from a piece of meat, you may then toss the meat to a dog.”59BT Niddah 31a Peirush:When you take the salt out of the meat, it only becomes fit for a dog. We learn in Avot D”Rebbe Natan: All those who dwell in the world enter the world with a cry and leave the world with a cry. They enter with their hands clenched and leave the world with their hands open. Why do they enter with their hands clenched and leave with them open? (When they enter, it is as if they say,) “The whole world is mine.” And when they leave, it is as if they say,” You may take everything I have acquired.”60This statement is not found in Pirkei D’Rebbe Natan but a similar one is found in Kohelet Rabbah 5:14 and Semachot, 3:1

“Who created within humans many openings,” (nikavim nikavim) is based on the verse, “Mined (nikavecha) for you, prepared the day you were created.” (Ez. 28:13)61The meaning of the verse is not clear. Some translations state, “the workmanship of thy settings and thy sockets was in thee, in the day that thou wast created they were prepared.” (Koren) “And many cavities,” (chalim chalim) is based on, “And hollows (michilot) in the ground.” (Is. 2:19) Some read it chalulim chalulim, but this is an error, for chalulim is an averbal noun (a gerund),62Literally: “noun of action.” it refers to a verbal noun—a word that comes from a verb and expresses the act of doing something. It is similar to an English gerund or action noun, like “running,” “writing,” “breaking,” “translation,” etc. standard nouns are words that are not verbs or adjectives but things in the broad grammatical sense.. In contrast, chalim is a standard noun with the same pattern as other words. The second lamed (of chalulim) is assimilated into the first lamed with a dagesh. Know that nekavim (holes) are narrow and not broad, while chalim (cavities) are wide. We read in the Ch. 2 of Ohalot:63It should read “the first chapter…” see Ohalot 1:8 ‘There are 248 limbs in a human body: 30 in the foot, (that is) 6 for every toe, 10 in the ankle, 2 in the shin, 5 in the knee, 1 in the thigh, 3 in the hip, 11 ribs, 30 in the hand, [that is] 6 to every finger, 2 in the forearm, 2 in the elbow, 1 in the upper arm and 4 in the shoulder, [For a total of] 101 on the one side [of the body] and 101 on the other. 18 vertebrae in the spine, 9 in the head, 8 in the neck, 6 in the key of the heart, and 5 around the genitals.”
Peirush: Pisat Haregel is the sole of the foot, like the palm of the hand, as in the verse, “A cloud as small as a man’s hand is rising in the west.” (I ki. 18:44) In Aramaic, a man’s hand is called כְּפִיסַת יַד (Kepisat yad). Karsul (ankle) refers to the joint closest to the heel. Katlit refers to the hip, the thickest part of the thigh, the place in which the loin is attached to the body. Kaneh is the bone closest to the hand (forearm). Marpek is the elbow joint, from the expression, “His neck was broken (mifrakto).” (I Sam 4:18).64Possibly the shoulder Mafteach shel lev (key of the heart) - the lungs are like the key to the heart, since they opens a way for air to enter and to expel vapor. Nikvotav refers to the instruments of procreation.65The Hebrew terms explained in this paragraph are all terms used in Mishnah Ohalot 1:8.

“It is obvious and known before Your Throne of Glory” is a rabbinic expression used in many places. It is based on, “God reveals deep and hidden things, knows what is in the darkness.” (Dan. 2:22) It states, “Before Your Throne of Glory,” and it does not say, “Before You,” as is commonly said, since the place of souls is the Throne of Glory. “That if one of them is blocked or one is opened.” That is, if an organ is blocked, which is usually opened, such as the stomach, urinary tract, or intestines. Or if one of the organs were opened, which is usually closed, such as the navel or the intestinal tract, “It would be impossible to exist even for a short while.” Rabbi Meir of Rothenburg66Meir of Rothenburg (c. 1215 – 2 May 1293) was a German Rabbi and poet, as well as a major contributing author of the tosafot on Rashi's commentary on the Talmud. He was also the teacher of the Rosh, Rabbeinu Asher ben Yehiel. said that one should not say “Even for a short while,” for one can close one’s mouth for many hours, and still live. “Praised are you, Adonai, Who heals all beings,” is based on the verse, “I wounded, and I will heal.” (Deut. 32:39). “And performs wonders” is a verse (Jud. 13:19). For there are several great miracles that the Holy One performs while a fetus resides in the mother’s womb. When a person sits in a dark, narrow space, his soul becomes distressed. Yet an infant resides in its mother's belly for nine months without becoming distressed. It is found that God performs wondrous acts for him in His care, such that the womb is not crushed. Some commentators explain that the blessing states, “Healer of all flesh,” because the cavities which God created in humans served to remove the refuse of food, for if it remained in the stomach, one would die. Its removal (from the body) is a type of healing; this is the meaning of “Healer of all flesh.” It then says, “And who performs wonders,” because the Holy One picks out the good food and rejects the refuse. Or else, “Who performs wonders,” because we read in Niddah, Ch. 3, “Rav Ḥinnana bar Pappa taught: 'What is written: 'Who does great deeds beyond comprehension, wondrous deeds without number” (Job 9:10). Come and see that the attributes of flesh and blood are unlike the attributes of the Holy One. The attribute of flesh and blood is that if one puts an article in a flask that is tied and its opening faces upward, it is uncertain whether the item is preserved from getting lost, and it is uncertain whether it is not preserved. But the Holy One, Blessed be He, forms the fetus in a woman’s open womb, and its opening faces downward, and yet the fetus is preserved.” Another point is that when a person places an article on a scale, the heavier the item, the more it descends. But when the Holy One forms a fetus, the heavier the offspring gets, the more it ascends upward in the womb.”67BT Niddah 31a Peirush: For during the last three months the fetus resides in the upper chamber, as stated above. We learn: “Rabbi Tanḥuma began: 'For You are great and perform wonders'” (Ps. 86:10). Rabbi Tanḥum said: A wineskin, if it has a hole as small as the point of a needle, all its air will escape from it. Yet a human is made with numerous cavities and orifices, but air does not escape from him. Who can do so? It is “You, alone, God” (Ps. 86:10).68Bereshit Rabbah 1:3

This is also found in the Tanchuma.69This statement does not appear to be in the Tanchuma? “And throughout the day, when one relieves himself, there are those who say that for ketanim (urination) one recites only Asher Yatzar, and for gedolim (defecation)70Ketanim and Gedolim literally mean “small” matters and “large” matters. Abudraham uses the words here as an euphemism. Ketanim refers to "urination" and "gedolim" to "defication". one recites Al Netilat Yadayim (“Regarding the washing of hands”) first, and there are those who say that whether for gedolim or ketanim, one recites both Al Netilat Yadayim and Asher Yatzar, for whenever one recites Asher Yatzar, which is a matter of sanctity, one must (first) recite Al Netilat Yadayim.” The Rosh asks this question a responsa, and this is what he writes: “If a person relieved himself in the morning and wiped, or urinated and rubbed (his hands), and wishes to pray, he should wash his hands and recite the blessing. But for the rest of the day, when he relieves himself or urinates, even if he wishes to study (Torah), he should not recite the blessing al netilat yadayim, but only Asher Yatzar. End quote.” Now, the custom is, in the morning, to recite both al netilat yadayim and Asher Yatzar, whether or not one relieves himself, because an impure spirit rests on the hands, and additionally because the hands are active (constantly touching things). It is impossible that one's hands did not come into contact with an unclean area at night. Furthermore, one is like the kohen gadol, who sanctifies himself by washing his hands before he serves the Creator, so that he might serve God with clean hands. Also, it is customary to rinse out one’s mouth because of the discharges with it, since one needs to mention God’s great name in a state of holiness and purity.

Rabbi Yaakov ben HaRosh writes that one must rinse one’s hands three times because an evil spirit dwells on the hands before washing, and it is not removed until one has poured the water (on them) three times. Therefore, one must refrain from allowing one’s hands to touch one's mouth, nose, ears, or eyes because the evil spirit dwells on them - end of quote.71Tur, Orech Chaim 4:1 There are four things for which the washing of the hands is needed; the mnemonic for them is, shetafatni - “And the flood overwhelms me.” (Ps. 69:3). Peirush: Shema - reciting the Shema, Tibul - dipping in liquid, Pat - bread, and Tefilah reciting the Amidah. Netilat Yadaim: all of these require washing the hands. We say in Shabbat Ch. 19 (Rabbe Eliezer d’milah): “Shmuel said: One who washes his face and does not wipe it will develop sores on his flesh. What is his remedy? Let him wash extensively in beet water.”72BT Shabbat 133a-b Rashi explains, “The skin of his face cracks. And I say that it is a kind of boil. And regarding ḥeres (חרס), which is written in the Torah (Deut. 28), ḥaspanita is the Aramaic translation of ḥeres (‘potsherd’)” - end quote. The water must come through the force of a person. If he has no water and fears that the time for prayer will pass, he may clean his hands with a pebble or with earth and recite the blessing “al nikayot yadayim” (“concerning the cleanliness of the hands”), based on the verse “I will wash my hands in cleanliness” (Psalms), etc. And so wrote the Rosh.

Afterwards, one recites, “My God, the soul you placed within me,” Elohai Neshamah. This blessing does not begin with Baruch, but not because it is an adjacent blessing73A Berachah Semucha or a Bracha Hasemucha Lchaverta refers any brachah that is connected to previous brachah in a series doesn't start with a Baruch such as the Amidah or the Birkat HaMazon. In this case, even though Elohai neshamah appears after Asher Yatzar and does not begin with Baruch attah. It is not connected to Asher yatzar as Abudraham will explain. to the previous blessing Asher Yatzar, for we have said in Berachot, Ch. 9 (HaRoeh): “When one awakens, he recites: ‘My God, the soul.’”74BT Berachot 60b Asher Yatzar is said separately each time one attends to one’s needs. However, Ra’avad explains, that (Elohai neshama) is considered adjacent to the blessing, “Who makes the bands of sleep fall upon my eyes and slumber upon my eyelids,” and sleep is not considered an interruption because there are no activities (during sleep).75See BT Berachot 60b. This is the blessing one recites when one goes to sleep. In the Talmud, the very next passage deals with Elohai Neshama suggesting that the two blessings are connected. This explanation troubles me, since it is impossible that one never fulfilled the mitzvah of marital intimacy (before going to sleep) without conversing, as said in, Berachot, Ch. 9.76BT Berachot 62a See Rav kahana al… רַב כָּהֲנָא עָל, גְּנָא תּוּתֵיהּ פּוּרְיֵיהּ דְּרַב. שַׁמְעֵיהּ דְּשָׂח וְשָׂחַק וְעָשָׂה צְרָכָיו. The Talmud tells the story of Rav Kahana hiding under the bed of Rav to learn from his teacher's most private and intimate actions. He hears Rav conversing (sach) with his wife, laughing and doing “what was necessary.” This seems to be proof that one could speak even after reciting the bedtime blessings. The correct explanation according to Rabbeinu Tam is: Elohai does not begin with Baruch because it is a blessing of thanksgiving for having returned one’s soul so that one may go about one's activities in the morning and attend to one’s needs. For if one does not first preface the blessing with thanksgiving for that upon which the blessing takes effect, it would be considered a berachah levatalah (a blessing uttered in vain). Similarly, the blessing over rain—where we say, ‘We thank You for every single drop…’ does not open with Baruch because it is a blessing of thanksgiving for the benefit that will come in the future from the rains.”77BT Berachot of Berachot 5

One must pause briefly between the words Elohai (“My God”) and Neshama (“Soul”) so that it does not appear that one is not returning above to God, God forbid.78Meaning of passage is unclear.
